domains.summary: Zero-trust architecture and endpoint defense: never trust, always verify — identity-centric access, microsegmentation, continuous verification, and endpoint detection and response, following the principles of NIST SP 800-207. This is an independent study course; it confers no certificate and claims no affiliation with any institution.

scenarios.title: The VPN is not a moat
scenarios.situation: A company routes all remote access through a VPN and treats everything inside the corporate network as trusted. An attacker phishes one employee's VPN credentials and moves laterally for six weeks undetected.
scenarios.prompt: Which zero-trust principle was violated, and what replaces the VPN-centric model?
evidence: NIST's Zero Trust Architecture publication defines the core tenet: never trust, always verify. Access decisions are made per-session based on identity, device posture, and context — not on network location. 'Inside the network' is not a security property.
choices: Implicit trust by network location: the fix is identity- and context-based per-request authorization (a policy decision point evaluating user, device health, and resource sensitivity every session) instead of a one-time VPN gate with a trusted interior.
The principle of least privilege was violated; the fix is a bigger VPN with more bandwidth.
No principle was violated; VPNs are zero-trust by definition.
The violated principle is defense in depth; the fix is a second VPN inside the first.
scenarios.why: A VPN moves the perimeter; zero trust removes it. Every request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted based on who and what is asking right now — location contributes context, never trust.
scenarios.hint: If the attacker is already 'inside,' what should still stop them?

scenarios.title: The alert that cried wolf
scenarios.situation: An EDR console fires 400 'suspicious PowerShell' alerts per day. Analysts have started bulk-closing them without review. Last week a real ransomware precursor hid in the noise for three days.
choices: Tune detection to the environment: baseline normal PowerShell use, write allowlisted rules for admin tooling, escalate only anomalous command lines (encoded commands, obfuscated scripts, unusual parents) — alert fidelity beats alert volume, and bulk-closing is the failure to fix.
Disable the PowerShell rule entirely; PowerShell alerts are always false positives.
Hire more analysts to close the 400 alerts by hand each day.
Uninstall PowerShell from all endpoints to eliminate the alert source.
scenarios.why: Alert fatigue is a detection-engineering failure: every unactionable alert trains analysts to ignore the actionable ones. Zero trust assumes breach — which only works if the sensors that detect breach are trustworthy.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem too many attacks, or too little tuning?

scenarios.title: Flatland
scenarios.situation: A network scan shows 2,000 hosts on a single flat /16 with no internal segmentation. Server, workstation, printer, and IoT camera traffic all mix freely; any compromised host can reach any other on any port.
scenarios.prompt: What is the misconfiguration, and what is the fix?
evidence: Zero-trust architectures shrink implicit trust zones to the smallest practical scope — ideally per-workload — so a compromised host cannot move laterally. Flat networks grant every foothold the whole estate.
choices: Missing microsegmentation: the flat /16 gives every compromised host unrestricted lateral reach — segment by workload sensitivity (servers, workstations, IoT/printers isolated with default-deny between zones) so a foothold stays a foothold.
The subnet is too large; renumbering to a /24 will fix lateral movement.
Printers need static IPs; DHCP is the vulnerability.
There is no misconfiguration; flat networks are recommended for performance.
scenarios.why: Segmentation is blast-radius engineering: assume breach, then make sure the breach cannot walk. Default-deny between zones turns one compromised camera into an incident instead of an enterprise-wide event.
scenarios.hint: What does the attacker's second step require that you can deny?

scenarios.title: Whose laptop is that?
scenarios.situation: A contractor's personal laptop — no disk encryption, OS two years out of date — authenticates with valid credentials and receives full access to the customer database because the access policy checks only username and password.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the access decision?
evidence: Zero trust evaluates the subject AND the device: managed status, encryption, patch level, EDR health. Credentials prove who claims to be asking; posture proves what is asking — an untrusted device with valid credentials is still untrusted.
choices: Device trust evaluation: the policy must check device posture (managed, encrypted, patched, EDR-healthy) alongside identity — valid credentials on an unmanaged, unpatched device should get limited or no access to sensitive data.
Nothing is missing; valid credentials are sufficient for full access.
The contractor needs a stronger password; device state is irrelevant.
The database should be moved to the contractor's laptop for convenience.
scenarios.why: Identity answers 'who'; posture answers 'on what.' A policy that asks only the first question grants the keys to whoever holds the password, on whatever device they happen to own.
scenarios.hint: The credentials are valid — so what else must be true before access is granted?

scenarios.title: The service account that never sleeps
scenarios.situation: An audit finds a CI/CD service account with standing Domain Admin rights, a password unchanged in four years, used by twelve pipelines — three of which were decommissioned. The team says 'it works, don't touch it.'
scenarios.prompt: Apply least privilege and assume breach: what is the remediation plan?
choices: Eliminate standing privilege: inventory which pipelines actually need the account, scope each to just-in-time, time-bound, least-privilege credentials (short-lived tokens per pipeline), rotate or vault the secret, and remove the dead pipelines' access — 'it works' is not a security posture.
Change the password once and leave everything else as-is; rotation alone satisfies least privilege.
Grant the account Enterprise Admin so pipelines never hit permission errors.
Delete the CI/CD system; pipelines are inherently insecure.
scenarios.why: Standing privilege is pre-authorized breach: every always-on admin credential is an attacker asset waiting to be stolen. Just-in-time, scoped, expiring access gives pipelines what they need for minutes, not forever.
scenarios.hint: What does each pipeline need, for how long, and why does it still have it?

scenarios.title: Build or buy the policy engine?
scenarios.situation: A mid-size firm must choose: build a custom policy decision point (PDP) in-house, or buy a zero-trust network access (ZTNA) platform. Build costs 2 engineer-years and full maintenance liability; buy costs $180k/year with vendor lock-in and a 6-month migration.
choices: Decide on differentiation and risk: access policy enforcement is undifferentiated heavy lifting with high breach cost if wrong — buy the platform (faster, maintained, audited) unless access control is genuinely a core competency; then run a pilot measuring policy-change latency, incident response integration, and exit cost before committing.
Always build; vendor products are never trustworthy.
Always buy the cheapest option; price is the only criterion.
Defer the decision for two years; the VPN is fine until then.
scenarios.why: The trade is build-risk (you own every bug in your PDP, and auth bugs are breach bugs) versus buy-risk (lock-in, price, fit). For security infrastructure, 'boring and maintained' usually beats 'clever and yours' — measure the pilot, price the exit.
scenarios.hint: Which risk is cheaper to be wrong about: your own auth code, or a vendor contract?

scenarios.title: The contractor portal decision
scenarios.situation: 60 contractors need project-portal access for 6 months. Their devices are unmanaged. The proposal: full VPN accounts 'like employees, just time-limited.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the zero trust answer?
evidence: 60 unmanaged devices, external users, 6-month need, one portal.
Time-limited VPN — network access for unknown devices.
choices: Resource-portal access, not VPN: browser-based PEP to ONLY the project portal, strong identity (MFA), session controls (short lifetime, no download), time-bound to the contract, and enhanced monitoring. The device's unknown posture caps its tier — 'time-limited VPN' still grants network access to unmanaged devices, which violates device-trust principles regardless of duration. Duration limits WHEN; the portal limits WHAT AND WHERE
Approve the time-limited VPN; the time bound handles the risk
Deny all contractor access; security first
Give VPN but monitor it closely
scenarios.why: Time-limiting a VPN does not fix what the VPN grants: network-level access from an unknown device. Six months of network access is six months of lateral-movement opportunity — the duration bound addresses the calendar, not the trust model. Denying all access kills the business need (and spawns shadow IT). 'Monitored VPN' watches the breach without preventing it. The zero trust pattern for this population is purpose-built: the resource portal gives exactly the portal, nothing else, with identity and session controls matched to the risk. The principle: access scope follows the weakest verified signal — unknown device means app-only, no matter how trusted the human or how short the engagement.
scenarios.hint: Why does time-limiting a VPN not fix its trust problem?

scenarios.title: The flat OT network
scenarios.situation: The manufacturing OT network is flat: PLCs, HMIs, and engineering workstations on one segment, no firewalling, Windows XP HMIs. IT proposes 'extending zero trust to OT' by installing agents on the PLCs.
scenarios.prompt: What is the realistic OT approach?
evidence: PLCs (no agents possible), XP HMIs (unpatchable), 24/7 production, safety implications.
Agents on PLCs — technically impossible and operationally dangerous.
choices: OT zero trust is network-centric, not agent-centric: unidirectional gateways / data diodes where feasible, strict segmentation (cell/zone model per IEC 62443), jump-host/PAM-brokered access for engineers, passive monitoring (no active scanning — it crashes PLCs), and an allow-listed conduit inventory. Agents on PLCs is a non-starter (no OS to host them, real-time constraints, vendor warranties). The XP HMIs get isolated + monitored + a replacement plan, not an agent
Install the agents; the vendor will support it
OT cannot do zero trust; leave it alone
Air-gap it completely and call it done
scenarios.why: OT constraints are physical: PLCs run real-time firmware (no agent OS), active scanning can halt production lines, and uptime/safety outweigh IT security preferences. Agent fantasies ignore all three. 'Leave it alone' abandons critical infrastructure. Air gaps are usually mythical (the USB stick, the vendor remote-access, the historian's network link — gaps have bridges). The achievable OT program: zone/conduit segmentation (the OT-native model), unidirectional data flows where possible, brokered human access (no direct RDP to HMIs from IT), passive-only monitoring, and an asset inventory (you cannot protect uncounted PLCs). Zero trust principles apply — verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach — but the MECHANISMS are OT-adapted. Meet the plant where it lives.
scenarios.hint: How do zero trust principles translate to OT constraints?

domains.name: Zero Trust Architecture
domains.summary: Designing networks that never grant implicit trust: the NIST SP 800-207 tenets, identity-centric access, microsegmentation, software-defined perimeters, and continuous verification. Architecture-level thinking for containing breaches that perimeter defenses miss. This material confers no certificate and implies no vendor endorsement.

scenarios.title: The Core Idea
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks for a one-sentence definition of zero trust to anchor a new security program. Four candidate statements are on the table.
scenarios.prompt: Which statement captures zero trust correctly?
choices: Never trust, always verify — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and continuously validated regardless of network location
A strong firewall perimeter keeps everything inside it safe
All devices on the corporate LAN are trusted by default
Connecting through the VPN makes a device trusted
scenarios.why: Zero trust eliminates the idea of a trusted network: location on the LAN or VPN no longer implies trustworthiness. Every request — user, device, workload — must prove itself each time, because breaches routinely start inside the perimeter. The other options all restate the perimeter model that zero trust replaces.
scenarios.hint: What happened to the idea of a 'trusted' internal network?

scenarios.title: Identity Is the Perimeter
scenarios.situation: The company is now mostly remote. The old model — VPN into the office network, then broad internal access — has produced two incidents from compromised home machines this year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right first control to deploy?
evidence: Incident 1: compromised home PC -> VPN -> lateral movement to file shares.
Incident 2: stolen VPN credentials used from unknown device.
choices: Phishing-resistant MFA plus device posture checks, enforced per application session before any resource access
Longer, more complex VPN passwords
A larger, faster perimeter firewall
A policy trusting employee home Wi-Fi networks
scenarios.why: When the network cannot be trusted, identity and device health become the boundary. MFA (preferably phishing-resistant) proves who is asking; posture checks prove the device is healthy; per-session enforcement means trust is re-evaluated continuously. Longer VPN passwords do nothing against a compromised endpoint or stolen session.
scenarios.hint: If the network can't be trusted, what becomes the boundary?

scenarios.title: After the Breach
scenarios.situation: Ransomware entered through one phishing workstation and reached 400 hosts in hours. The post-incident review finds a flat /16 network: any host can talk to any host on any port.
scenarios.prompt: Which architectural change best contains the next incident?
evidence: Single flat VLAN: 10.0.0.0/16 — workstations, servers, printers, OT adjacent. No east-west filtering.
choices: Microsegmentation — enforce least-privilege east-west policy between workloads so a compromise cannot move laterally
Buy more antivirus licenses for the endpoints
Segment only the guest Wi-Fi — the servers are the priority
Air-gap everything and end remote work
scenarios.why: Flat networks let attackers move laterally at will — the blast radius becomes the whole enterprise. Microsegmentation carves the network into small trust zones with explicit allow-rules between them, so one compromised workstation cannot reach the server tier. It directly addresses the observed failure mode: uncontrolled east-west movement.
scenarios.hint: The attacker moved sideways — what controls sideways movement?

scenarios.title: Beyond the VPN
scenarios.situation: A third-party vendor needs access to exactly one internal application for a two-week project. The traditional answer is a full VPN tunnel into the corporate network.
scenarios.prompt: Which access model fits zero trust best?
choices: Software-defined perimeter / zero-trust network access: brokered, per-application, per-session access with no network-level trust granted
A full VPN tunnel — it is how vendor access has always been done
Publish the application's port directly to the internet
Email the vendor the data they need instead
scenarios.why: A VPN grants network-level access — far more than 'one application' — and makes the vendor's potentially unmanaged device an insider. SDP/ZTNA brokers access to the specific resource only, after verifying identity and device, with no implicit trust in the underlying network. Least privilege applied to connectivity itself.
scenarios.hint: What's the least access that still gets the job done — a network, or an application?

scenarios.title: Trust, but Continuously Verify
scenarios.situation: A user authenticated normally from headquarters at 9:00 AM. At 9:20, a login for the same account arrives from another continent on an unknown device, and immediately attempts the admin panel.
evidence: 09:00 MFA success — known device, HQ office
09:20 password-only success — unknown device, foreign ASN
choices: Step-up authentication and session re-evaluation — continuous verification challenges or revokes the session when risk signals appear mid-session
Do nothing — the session is valid for 8 hours once authenticated
Permanently block the user — no investigation needed
Only authenticate at login — that is the industry standard
scenarios.why: Zero trust treats authentication as a moment and authorization as continuous: the policy engine re-evaluates trust as context changes. Impossible travel plus a new device plus privilege escalation is exactly the signal set that should trigger step-up auth or session termination. Login-time-only checks leave an eight-hour window for the attacker.
scenarios.hint: Authentication is a moment — what should authorization be?

scenarios.title: The Policy Engine Decision
scenarios.situation: You are designing access policy for the finance application. Options range from a static IP allowlist to a fully dynamic model, and the team worries about complexity.
scenarios.prompt: Which model aligns with zero trust, and why is the complexity worth it?
choices: Attribute-based dynamic policy — user identity, device posture, location, and risk score evaluated per session by the policy engine; it adapts to real-time risk instead of freezing yesterday's assumptions
A static IP allowlist — simple to understand and audit
Identical access for everyone — fairness and simplicity
Annual access reviews only — least administrative overhead
scenarios.why: NIST SP 800-207's tenets require access determined by dynamic policy: the observable state of the identity, the device, and behavioral attributes, evaluated per session. Static rules cannot react to compromised credentials or devices — they encode trust decisions that go stale. The complexity is the point: it is what makes access decisions reflect current reality.
scenarios.hint: NIST says access is determined by dynamic policy — what does 'dynamic' have to buy you?

scenarios.title: The service account with the keys to everything
scenarios.situation: Discovery: a backup service account is a domain admin 'because the backup needs to read everything.' Its password is 4 years old, stored in 3 scripts and a wiki page.
evidence: Domain admin, 4-year password, in scripts + wiki. Purpose: read files for backup.
Read-only access to file data — not admin rights, not interactive logon.
choices: Scope to the actual need: replace domain admin with Backup Operators group membership (the designed privilege for backup — bypasses file ACLs for reading without admin rights), convert to a gMSA (no managed password, cannot be pasted into wikis), remove interactive logon rights, and rotate immediately (the wiki copy is burned). 'Needs to read everything' never meant 'needs to ADMINISTER everything'
Rotate the password; the rights are needed
The backup software requires domain admin; keep it
Delete the account; backups can run as SYSTEM
scenarios.why: Domain admin for a read job is the canonical over-privilege: the task needs file-read bypass (Backup Operators), not directory administration. Rotating the password keeps the excessive rights (and the next wiki paste). 'Software requires DA' is almost always false — test with Backup Operators; vendors spec DA out of laziness. SYSTEM has its own issues (local-only identity, still over-broad). The gMSA conversion kills the password-in-wiki class permanently (no password to leak). And the burned credential rotates NOW, not at the next cycle — the wiki page was readable by everyone with wiki access for years. Least privilege is job-description-shaped: read the job, grant the shape, nothing more.
scenarios.hint: What is the designed privilege for backup read access?

scenarios.title: The allow-all firewall rule
scenarios.situation: The 'temporary' firewall rule from the 2021 cloud migration — allow 0.0.0.0/0 to the app tier — is still live. 'Nobody wanted to break the migration by removing it.'
evidence: The app tier — behind 'zero trust' — is internet-reachable.
choices: Stale allows destroy microsegmentation: the rule must die immediately (scope to the actual migration source long gone, or remove), and the lifecycle that allowed 3-year 'temporary' rules must be fixed — every allow with owner, reason, expiry; automation enforcing expiry; quarterly reviews. A microsegmented architecture with a 0.0.0.0/0 hole is a flat network with extra steps and extra cost
The migration might still need it; keep it
Narrow it slightly to be safe
Microsegmentation does not work in cloud
scenarios.why: 'Might still need it' after 3 years is fear without evidence — check the flow logs (nothing from 0.0.0.0/0 but scanners, guaranteed). Slight narrowing keeps the hole. Cloud is where microsegmentation is EASIEST (security groups are code). The real lesson: the organization paid for segmentation architecture and got flat-network exposure, because rules have no lifecycle. The fix is the unglamorous machinery: rule-as-code with expiries, automated enforcement, quarterly attestation, and a culture where 'temporary' means 'with an expiry date or it does not ship.' Every allow-list is a garden; without weeding, it returns to jungle — and jungles have predators.
scenarios.hint: What does a 0.0.0.0/0 rule do to a microsegmented design?

scenarios.title: The TLS that was blamed
scenarios.situation: After enabling TLS on internal service traffic, p99 latency rises 8%. The team proposes disabling internal TLS 'for performance.'
evidence: p99 +8% with TLS 1.3, session resumption enabled. No tuning attempted.
Disable internal encryption to recover the 8%.
choices: 8% is the START of tuning, not a verdict: enable session resumption/tickets (done), check cipher selection (AES-GCM with hardware accel vs ChaCha), verify no handshake-per-request anti-patterns (connection reuse), and measure against the SECURITY value (tenet 2 — internal plaintext is a finding). Disabling encryption trades a tunable 8% for permanent exposure. The question is never 'TLS or speed' — it is 'tuned TLS,' which is usually 1–3%
Disable it; 8% matters at scale
The measurement is wrong; TLS is free
Buy faster CPUs to absorb it
scenarios.why: TLS overhead is overwhelmingly in handshakes, not bulk crypto — with session resumption and connection reuse, steady-state cost is typically 1–3%, and the 8% here signals untuned configuration (handshake per request is the usual culprit), not physics. Disabling internal TLS reintroduces the exact exposure tenet 2 forbids — and 'at scale' the 8% costs less than one breach. 'TLS is free' is false (it is cheap, not free — honesty matters). Faster CPUs treat the symptom expensively. The engineering answer: profile (where is the 8%? handshakes, presumably), tune (resumption, reuse, cipher choice), re-measure, and THEN decide — with the security requirement as a constraint, not a variable. Performance work and security work are both engineering; do both.
scenarios.hint: Where does TLS latency actually come from, and how is it tuned?

domains.name: NIST SP 800-207 Tenets
domains.summary: The seven tenets of zero trust architecture and the logical components: policy engine, policy administrator, policy enforcement point.

scenarios.title: The VPN upgrade proposal
scenarios.situation: The network team proposes 'upgrading' the VPN concentrators for $200k to 'improve zero trust posture' — faster VPN, same architecture: connect, get network access, browse freely.
scenarios.prompt: How does this score against the tenets?
evidence: Bigger VPN pipes; authentication at connect; full LAN access after; no per-app policy; no device checks.
T3 per-session: fail. T4 dynamic policy: fail. T6 enforce-before-access per resource: fail.
choices: It fails the tenets it claims to serve: a faster VPN is still network-location trust — tenets 3 (per-session), 4 (dynamic policy), and 6 (enforce before each resource access) all fail. The $200k should fund identity (SSO+MFA), a ZTNA pilot, and device compliance — the tenets' actual requirements. Speed never fixed a trust model
Approve it; faster VPN is a zero trust improvement
Approve half; the VPN still has a role for legacy
Reject it; VPNs are banned in zero trust
scenarios.why: The tenets are a design linter: run the proposal through them and it fails three of seven. 'Faster' does not change WHAT the VPN grants (network access on connect) — the trust model is identical, just quicker. Approving half still funds the wrong architecture. 'Banned' overstates it (VPNs retain legacy/break-glass roles), but the budget priority is clear: identity, per-app access, device signals. The general skill: evaluate every security purchase against the tenets BEFORE the vendor demo — tenet failures are visible on paper, no POC needed.
scenarios.hint: Which tenets does a traditional VPN violate?

scenarios.title: The PEP after the resource
scenarios.situation: A 'zero trust' product is deployed: users authenticate to a portal, then get full network routes to the data center. The vendor calls the portal the PEP. An attacker with valid creds scans the entire data-center network.
evidence: Portal authenticates, then grants NETWORK access. Scanning/enumeration possible post-auth.
Enforcement must be BEFORE each resource access, per session — not once before network access.
choices: The PEP is in the wrong place: tenet 6 requires enforcement before EACH resource access — a portal that grants network routes is a VPN with a nicer login. The correct architecture puts PEPs per resource (proxies/gateways/agents in front of each app), so the attacker's valid creds yield only the specific authorized sessions, with no network to scan
The portal needs stronger authentication
Network scanning should be blocked by IDS
The product is fine; the attacker had valid creds
scenarios.why: This is the most common 'zero trust' product failure: authentication at a portal followed by network-level access recreates the VPN's trust model exactly — the tenets are violated at tenet 6 (enforce before access, per resource). Stronger auth does not fix it (the attacker HAD valid creds — that is the assume-breach case). IDS detects scanning; it does not prevent the access that enables it. 'Valid creds' is not a defense — the architecture must contain valid-creds attackers (that is the entire point of assume breach + per-resource PEPs). The test for any ZTNA claim: with stolen creds, what can the attacker REACH? If the answer is 'the network,' it is not zero trust.
scenarios.hint: Where must the PEP sit relative to the resource?

scenarios.title: The static contractor grant
scenarios.situation: A contractor got VPN + database access for a 3-month project — 14 months ago. The grant is still active. Nobody reviewed it. The contractor's company was breached last month.
scenarios.prompt: Which tenets failed, and what is the fix?
evidence: Static, permanent, unreviewed. No device checks, no time bounds, no monitoring of the contractor's sessions.
T4 (dynamic policy): fail — static grant. T5 (monitor all): fail — unmonitored. T7 (learn): fail — no review.
choices: Tenets 4, 5, and 7 failed together: the fix is time-bound, signal-driven access — grant with expiry tied to the contract, device posture checks per session, session logging reviewed, and automatic deprovisioning at contract end. The breach at the contractor's company is exactly the event dynamic policy exists for: their risk changed, so their access should have re-evaluated
Remove the contractor's access now; problem solved
Contractors should not get database access at all
The breach was at their company, not ours; no action needed
scenarios.why: Removing access now fixes the instance but not the pattern — the next contractor gets the same permanent grant. Banning contractor DB access ignores business reality (they were hired for database work). 'Their breach, not ours' misses that the contractor's credentials are YOUR attack surface (their compromise becomes your session). The tenet-driven fix addresses the systemic failure: access with lifetimes (contracts end), live signals (their company's breach should have triggered re-evaluation), and monitoring (someone should have noticed 14 months). Dynamic policy means access reflects CURRENT risk, not the risk on the day the ticket was approved. Every grant needs an expiry; every expiry needs an owner.
scenarios.hint: What should happen to access when the subject's risk changes?

scenarios.title: The logs nobody reads
scenarios.situation: The company collects extensive logs (firewall, proxy, IdP) into a SIEM — which nobody monitors. The dashboards exist; the alerts are unconfigured. A breach investigation finds the attacker's lateral movement IN the logs, unnoticed for 5 months.
evidence: Logs collected, retained, unexamined. No detections, no reviews, no one assigned.
T5 (monitor integrity/security of all assets): fail — collection without analysis is not monitoring. T7 (use info to improve posture): fail — the data never improved anything.
choices: Tenets 5 and 7: monitoring means ANALYSIS, not storage — and the security posture must IMPROVE from what is learned. The fix: detection engineering on the collected data (start with 5 high-value detections), assigned ownership (someone's job, not everyone's hobby), and a feedback loop (findings → policy changes). The 5-month dwell time is the tuition for 'collect and ignore'
Collect more logs; the SIEM needs more data
The SIEM product is inadequate; replace it
Five months is normal dwell time; accept it
scenarios.why: Tenet 5 says monitor — the verb implies watching, analyzing, acting. A SIEM as a write-only archive satisfies compliance checkboxes while missing breaches for 5 months. More logs into an unmonitored SIEM just buries the signal deeper. Product replacement without ownership and detections reproduces the failure expensively. Accepting 5-month dwell normalizes failure. The fix is operational, not technical: detections (start with the attacks you most fear), ownership (named humans), and the tenet-7 loop (every finding improves a policy or detection). Monitoring is a human+process system with tool support — the tool was never the missing piece.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between log collection and monitoring?

scenarios.title: The DNS server exemption
scenarios.situation: The zero trust rollout covers users and servers — but 'infrastructure' (DNS, NTP, AD, the network gear itself) is exempted as 'too critical to touch.' An attacker compromises the (unmonitored) DNS server and redirects internal traffic.
evidence: Infrastructure services: no PEP, no monitoring, implicit trust. Rationale: 'we cannot risk breaking DNS.'
ALL data sources and computing services are resources — no exemptions for plumbing.
choices: Tenet 1: there are no exempt infrastructure services — DNS, NTP, and directory services are resources subject to the same access control and monitoring. The 'too critical to touch' rationale inverts reality: the most critical services need the MOST protection, applied carefully (lab-tested, phased), not exemption. The attacker understood tenet 1 better than the architects
DNS cannot be in zero trust scope; it is too foundational
Monitor it but do not enforce on it
The attacker was sophisticated; exemptions are normal
scenarios.why: Tenet 1's 'all' is absolute: every data source and computing service is a resource. Exempting DNS/NTP/AD creates the exact blind spot attackers exploit — infrastructure is high-value precisely because everything depends on it. 'Too critical to touch' is how the most critical systems become the least protected; the correct approach is careful inclusion (test in lab, phase the rollout, monitor first). Monitoring without enforcement is half a control (you will watch the next attack too). Sophistication is irrelevant — DNS hijacking is a standard technique against exactly this kind of exemption. The lesson generalizes: every exemption list is an attacker's target list. Minimize exemptions; document, monitor, and expire the ones that remain.
scenarios.hint: Why are infrastructure exemptions attacker targets?

scenarios.title: The 8-hour ticket
scenarios.situation: Users authenticate each morning and get an 8-hour session to everything. At 2 PM, a user's laptop is compromised. The attacker rides the valid session until 5 PM — no re-verification occurs.
scenarios.prompt: What does per-session access require here?
evidence: 8 hours, single morning verification, no mid-session checks.
Access is per-session: each session authenticated, authorized, and re-evaluated — not once per workday.
choices: Shorter, re-evaluated sessions: tenet 3 means the 9 AM decision does not cover 2 PM. Implement session lifetimes matched to risk (shorter for sensitive apps), continuous device-posture checks, and revocation that propagates when signals flip (EDR alert → sessions die). The 8-hour ticket is the VPN-era model with SSO paint
Require re-authentication every 15 minutes for everyone
The EDR should have prevented the compromise
8 hours is standard; the user should have reported faster
scenarios.why: Per-session does not mean harass-the-user every 15 minutes — it means trust is continuously earned, not granted at 9 AM and assumed until 5. The mechanisms: risk-calibrated session lengths, background re-verification (device posture, behavior), and tested revocation (the 2 PM EDR alert must kill the 9 AM session). EDR preventing the compromise is ideal but assume-breach says plan for its failure. Faster user reporting is nice but not a control. The architecture must handle 'valid session, compromised endpoint' — because that is the common case, not the edge. Tenet 3's operational form: sessions have lifetimes, signals are re-checked, and revocation works.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between per-session and per-day trust?

scenarios.title: The plaintext backup stream
scenarios.situation: Database backups stream to object storage over the internal network — unencrypted ('it never leaves our network'). A network tap at the cloud interconnect captures months of backups.
evidence: Backup traffic: plaintext, justified by network location.
ALL communication is secured, regardless of network location.
choices: Tenet 2 has no 'internal' exception: the backup stream must be encrypted in transit (TLS) AND the backup data encrypted at rest — defense in depth for the crown jewels. 'Never leaves our network' was false (cloud interconnect) and irrelevant (tenet 2 does not care about location). The tap captured months because nothing was encrypted at either layer
The network tap is the problem; secure the interconnect facility
Internal traffic encryption is overkill; segment the backup network instead
Encrypt the storage; transit encryption is redundant
scenarios.why: Tenet 2's 'all communication' includes the backup stream, the replication link, and the management protocols — location never enters the reasoning. The facility will always have SOME risk (insiders, misconfigurations, lawful access); encryption makes the captured bits useless. Segmentation helps but does not replace encryption (defense in depth, not either/or). Encrypting only at rest leaves the transit window open — the tap proved it. The pattern to internalize: every plaintext flow is a finding, regardless of which network it traverses. Scan for them (the 10-minute capture test), encrypt them, verify with captures. 'Internal' is a routing fact, not a security property.
scenarios.hint: Does tenet 2 have an 'internal network' exception?

domains.name: Identity as the Perimeter
domains.summary: Strong identity for users, devices, and workloads: MFA, phishing-resistant auth, and identity-aware access decisions.

scenarios.title: The SIM-swap
scenarios.situation: The CFO's SMS-based MFA is bypassed via SIM swap; the attacker resets the email password and reads M&A documents for 3 days before detection.
evidence: SMS codes. Attack: carrier SIM swap (social engineering), codes intercepted.
Email takeover → document access → 3 days undetected.
choices: SMS is not phishing-resistant MFA: SIM swap and interception defeat it routinely — for high-value targets (executives, admins, finance), require FIDO2/WebAuthn, which is origin-bound and cannot be intercepted or replayed. The 3-day dwell also indicts monitoring (no impossible-travel or new-device alerts?). Fix both: upgrade the MFA method AND the detection
SMS MFA is standard; the carrier is at fault
The CFO should have noticed the phone losing service
MFA cannot stop determined attackers
scenarios.why: SMS MFA's threat model collapsed years ago: SIM swapping is a commoditized attack (carrier support social engineering), and SMS interception is routine. For the CFO — the highest-value target — SMS MFA was a paper wall. FIDO2's origin-binding kills both SIM swap and phishing: the credential only works on the real site, and there is nothing to intercept. Blaming the carrier outsources your security to a phone company's support desk. User vigilance is not a control. 'Cannot stop determined attackers' surrenders the exact ground FIDO2 holds — it DOES stop these attackers. The rule: MFA strength must match target value; executives and admins get phishing-resistant methods, period.
scenarios.hint: Why does FIDO2 survive attacks that kill SMS MFA?

scenarios.title: The 14 accounts
scenarios.situation: A departing employee's SSO is disabled Friday. Six months later, audit finds 3 still-active accounts: the expense tool (SSO never configured), the code repo (personal token), and the VPN (separate credential).
evidence: SSO covers ~80% of apps. Leaver process: disable IdP only.
Non-federated apps, personal tokens, and parallel credentials survive IdP disable.
choices: The identity perimeter has holes: every non-federated app, personal access token, and parallel credential is a deprovisioning gap. Fix: complete the SSO/federation rollout (every app federated or explicitly exceptioned), inventory and revoke personal tokens at offboard, eliminate parallel credentials (one identity per human), and AUDIT leavers (sample check 30 days after). 'Disabled in the IdP' must mean 'disabled everywhere' — verify it
The offboarding checklist was not followed; retrain HR
Three accounts in 6 months is acceptable
Disable the accounts now; the process works
scenarios.why: Disabling now fixes three accounts; the SYSTEM still produces them. Retraining does not fix a process that relies on humans remembering 14 systems. 'Acceptable' normalizes a breach vector (ex-employee access is a classic initial-access path). The identity perimeter is only as complete as its coverage: SSO at 80% means 20% of access lives outside the perimeter's control. The program: federate everything feasible, exception-document the rest (with compensating offboard steps), kill parallel credentials, automate token revocation, and verify with post-leaver audits. Deprovisioning is the identity perimeter's most important operation — it must be complete, fast, and verified, not just initiated.
scenarios.hint: Why is SSO coverage percentage a security metric?

scenarios.title: The 47 push notifications
scenarios.situation: An attacker with the user's password spams 47 MFA push notifications at 3 AM; the half-asleep user approves one. Full account takeover.
scenarios.prompt: What failed, and what is the fix?
evidence: Push-based, no number matching, no context shown.
MFA fatigue / push bombing — the user is the vulnerability.
choices: Push without safeguards fails open to human exhaustion: fix with number matching (user must enter the number shown on the login screen — a spammed push shows a number the attacker cannot know... actually the attacker CAN relay it; the real fixes are layered), but the durable answer is phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) where there is nothing to approve-fatigue, PLUS anomaly detection (47 pushes at 3 AM should auto-block and alert). Push bombing exploits the approval UX — remove the UX or guard it
The user needs security training
Disable MFA; it clearly does not work
Limit pushes to business hours
scenarios.why: MFA fatigue turns the human into the bypass: 47 pushes at 3 AM will eventually get an approve-tap from anyone. Training helps but does not fix a UX that allows unlimited 3 AM pushes. Disabling MFA is surrender. Business-hours limits break legitimate off-hours work. The layered fix: (1) number matching raises the bar (attacker must relay the number in real time — harder, though not impossible), (2) anomaly detection auto-blocks impossible patterns (47 pushes, 3 AM, new location) and alerts, (3) the end state is FIDO2, where authentication is a cryptographic ceremony with no approve-button to fatigue. Push MFA was a step up from passwords; it is not the destination. Treat push-bombing as a known attack pattern with known defenses, not a user failure.
scenarios.hint: Why is push-button MFA vulnerable to fatigue attacks?

scenarios.title: The 5-year-old password
scenarios.situation: Discovery finds 40 service accounts with passwords unchanged in 5+ years, several with domain admin rights, one used by a vendor whose contract ended in 2021.
evidence: 40 stale service accounts; 6 domain admins; 1 ex-vendor; passwords in config files and scripts across the fleet.
Each is a valid credential an attacker can use indefinitely — no MFA, no expiry, no monitoring.
choices: Service accounts are identities outside the identity perimeter: bring them in — inventory every one (owner, purpose, scope), eliminate standing privilege (JIT or managed identities), rotate to short-lived/machine-managed credentials (gMSA, managed identities, workload identity federation), kill the ex-vendor's immediately, and monitor their use (a service account logging in interactively is an alert). The 5-year password is a 5-year-valid breach key
Service accounts cannot use MFA; nothing can be done
Rotate the passwords now; that fixes it
The vendor account is the only real problem
scenarios.why: 'Cannot use MFA' is not the end of the discussion — it is the beginning of workload identity (managed identities, gMSA, short-lived tokens, none of which need human MFA). Rotating now resets the clock but keeps the pattern (static, long-lived, unmonitored). The ex-vendor account is the scariest instance, not the only problem — the other 39 are equally valid credentials. The program: every service account gets an owner and a purpose (or it dies), privileges scoped to the job (no service account needs domain admin — prove otherwise), credentials managed by machines (gMSA/managed identity, not humans typing passwords into configs), and usage monitored (service accounts do not log in interactively, browse the web, or work at 3 AM — anomalies alert). Workload identity deserves the same rigor as human identity.
scenarios.hint: How do you apply 'identity as the perimeter' to service accounts?

scenarios.title: The engineer-turned-manager
scenarios.situation: An engineer promoted to manager 2 years ago retains prod database access, VPN admin, and the deploy keys 'just in case.' Their team now includes contractors. Their account is phished.
evidence: Role changed 2 years ago; entitlements never reviewed. Phished account had prod + admin + deploy.
Contractor-adjacent manager account with full technical access — maximum damage.
choices: The mover process and access reviews: role changes must trigger entitlement re-evaluation (remove what the new role does not need), and periodic certifications must catch what the process missed. 'Just in case' is privilege accretion — the manager's risk profile changed (more phishing-targeted, broader team) while access stayed at engineer-plus. Fix: mover-triggered reviews, quarterly certifications with real attestation (not approve-all), and the phished account's blast radius as the cautionary tale
The user should not have been phished; more training
Managers need prod access for emergencies
Promotions should not change access
scenarios.why: Training does not fix structural over-privilege — the phish was the trigger, the 2-year-old entitlements were the loaded weapon. 'Emergency' access is what JIT and break-glass are for, not standing grants. Promotions absolutely should change access (the job changed; the access must follow). The failed processes: (1) mover workflow — HR role change should auto-trigger access review; (2) certifications — someone should have attested (or removed) those grants in 2 years of quarters; (3) the 'just in case' culture — every standing grant needs a current justification. Least privilege is temporal as well as scoped: access must track the CURRENT role, not the resume. Automate the mover trigger; make certifications consequential (unattested access expires).
scenarios.hint: Why are role changes (movers) the highest-risk JML event?

scenarios.title: The silent break-glass
scenarios.situation: The break-glass domain admin account was used last Tuesday. Nobody knows by whom or why. It is not monitored — 'it is for emergencies, we do not want alerts waking people.'
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this break-glass design?
evidence: Break-glass DA, password in a sealed envelope (last changed 2019), no alerting on use.
Used Tuesday; discovered Friday during an unrelated review.
choices: Break-glass must be LOUD: every use pages the security team immediately — the whole point is that legitimate use is rare and announced, so any unannounced use is an incident. Silent break-glass is a stealth admin account. Fix: alert on any authentication, rotate the credential after each use (or on schedule), store it properly (not a 2019 envelope), and require post-use incident review. 'Do not wake people' inverts the purpose
Break-glass accounts should not exist; remove it
The envelope system works; just check it more often
Change the password yearly; that is sufficient
scenarios.why: Break-glass exists for 'the PAM is down and the building is on fire' — scenarios so rare that ANY use is newsworthy. Silent use means you cannot distinguish emergency from compromise, which makes the account a perfect attacker target (highest privilege, no monitoring, stale credential). Removing it entirely leaves no recovery path when PAM fails. Envelope-checking does not detect USE (the envelope was sealed; the account was used — the credential was copied long ago). Yearly rotation without use-alerting still leaves 364 silent days. The design: monitored like a fire alarm (use = page), credential secured and rotated, every use followed by a review ('was this the emergency we designed for?'). Loud by design, or it is a backdoor.
scenarios.hint: Why must break-glass use trigger an immediate alert?

scenarios.title: The stale SAML app
scenarios.situation: A vendor relationship ended 2 years ago, but their SaaS app's SAML trust to the company IdP is still active. The vendor was acquired by a competitor last year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the federation hygiene failure?
evidence: SAML app registration active, 2 years post-contract. The acquirer (competitor) now controls the vendor's side.
Anyone the acquirer authenticates via that trust gets YOUR app's assertions — the trust outlived the relationship.
choices: Federation lifecycle management: app registrations are access grants and must follow the vendor lifecycle — contract ends → trust disabled (immediately), then deleted after data-transition. The acquirer angle makes it urgent: the trust now authenticates a competitor's users into your systems. Fix now: disable the trust, audit what it accessed, then build the offboarding checklist (SAML/OIDC trusts included) and review all app registrations quarterly
SAML trusts are harmless without user accounts
The competitor would not bother attacking via this
Deleting it might break something; leave it
scenarios.why: A SAML trust IS the access: it says 'I accept this IdP's word about who users are.' Active trust + their IdP = their users get your assertions — no local accounts needed. 'They would not bother' is not a security control. 'Might break something' after 2 years of disuse is fear without evidence (and disproves itself: nothing has used it in 2 years). The systemic fix: vendor offboarding includes identity offboarding (disable federation trusts, revoke API keys, remove SSO apps) on a checklist, owned by whoever owns the vendor relationship, verified by security. And the quarterly app-registration review catches the ones the checklist missed. Trusts are grants; grants have lifecycles.
scenarios.hint: Why is a SAML trust an access grant even without local accounts?

domains.name: Device Trust & Health
domains.summary: Device posture, compliance, EDR signals, and certificates as access-decision inputs.

scenarios.title: The contractor laptop
scenarios.situation: 50 contractors need the project portal. Their devices are unmanaged (no MDM, unknown patch state, unknown EDR). The project starts Monday. IT proposes 'just give them VPN like employees.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct device-trust posture?
evidence: 50 unmanaged devices, unknown health, external users, sensitive project data.
VPN with employee-level network access — full trust for unknown devices.
choices: Tiered access for unmanaged devices: resource-portal (browser-based) access to ONLY the project portal, with strong identity (MFA), session controls (short lifetime, no download or watermarked), and enhanced monitoring — NOT VPN network access. The device's unknown posture caps its trust tier; the portal model exists precisely for this population. 'Like employees' confuses employment with device trust
Give them VPN; the project deadline matters most
Buy 50 managed laptops by Monday
Deny all access; unmanaged devices are banned
scenarios.why: VPN-for-contractors grants network access based on identity alone — the device (unknown patch, unknown EDR, possibly compromised) rides along with full trust. That inverts the device-trust model. Buying 50 laptops by Monday is fantasy procurement. Banning access kills the project (the business will route around you). The resource-portal pattern is the designed answer: no agent to deploy, no network to join, per-app sessions with strong identity and session-level controls, and the data stays in the portal (no local copies on unknown devices). The principle: access tier follows the WEAKEST verified signal — unknown device means constrained access, regardless of how trusted the human is. Deadline pressure does not change the threat model.
scenarios.hint: What access tier do unmanaged devices get, and why?

scenarios.title: The agent that went quiet
scenarios.situation: A user's laptop stops reporting to EDR (agent crashed). The user still has full access for 3 days until helpdesk fixes the agent. During the window, the laptop is infected via a malicious ad.
evidence: EDR silent 3 days; access unchanged; infection during the blind window.
'No data' treated as neutral — access continued.
choices: Unknown posture = untrusted: 'agent not reporting' must degrade access (deny or step-down to a remediation tier), not continue it. The 3-day blind window with full access is exactly when attackers operate — killing the agent is step one of many playbooks. Fix: posture-freshness requirements (signal older than X = untrusted), automated remediation prompts, and SOC alerting on agent silence for high-risk users
The agent crashing is an IT reliability issue, not security
The user should have reported the EDR icon missing
Antivirus would have caught it anyway
scenarios.why: Treating missing telemetry as neutral is a fail-open design: the attacker's first move (kill the sensor) becomes invisible AND consequence-free. The infection during the window is not bad luck — it is the predictable result. Agent reliability matters, but the security architecture must assume sensor failure (hostile or accidental) and fail closed. User reporting is not a control. 'Antivirus would have caught it' is speculation about a different layer. The zero trust answer: trust requires FRESH, POSITIVE evidence of health — absence of evidence is evidence of absence (of trust). Build the freshness requirement into policy: stale signal = untrusted = reduced access until remediated. The EDR icon is not the control; the policy engine's response to silence is.
scenarios.hint: In a zero trust model, what does missing telemetry mean?

scenarios.title: The rooted phone
scenarios.situation: An executive's Android phone is rooted (for 'customization'). It has the email app with cached M&A documents, enrolled as a BYOD device with basic MDM.
evidence: Rooted: security model compromised — any app can read others' data, MDM controls bypassable.
Cached sensitive documents on a device whose OS integrity is void.
choices: Rooted/jailbroken = untrusted, immediately: revoke the device's access (wipe the managed container / revoke tokens and certs), require a compliant device for re-enrollment, and treat the cached documents as potentially exposed (they were readable by any process on that phone). 'Customization' does not survive the threat model — root breaks the app sandboxing that BYOD data protection depends on
It is the executive's personal phone; allow it with a warning
The MDM says compliant; trust the MDM
Have them unroot it and continue
scenarios.why: Rooting destroys the OS security model: sandboxing, permission checks, and MDM enforcement all become advisory — malware (or a curious app) reads the email app's cache freely. An MDM reporting 'compliant' on a rooted device is either misconfigured or being lied to (root can spoof attestation). Executive status does not change the physics. 'Unroot and continue' leaves the exposure window unaddressed (what already read the cache?) and trusts the same user judgment that rooted it. The response: revoke access NOW (container wipe + token/cert revocation), assess document exposure, re-enroll only on a compliant device, and make the policy explicit — rooted/jailbroken devices are categorically untrusted, no exceptions, no matter whose pocket they are in.
scenarios.hint: Why does rooting void BYOD data protections?

scenarios.title: The WiFi cert cliff
scenarios.situation: The fleet's WiFi machine certificates expire Saturday (issued 3 years ago, 3-year validity, no auto-renewal). Monday: thousands cannot connect to corporate WiFi. The helpdesk is drowning.
evidence: Machine certs, 3-year life, manual issuance at provision, no renewal process, no expiry monitoring.
Fleet-wide auth failure on a predictable date — the most avoidable outage class.
choices: Certificate lifecycle automation: auto-enrollment with auto-renewal (AD CS autoenrollment, MDM/SCEP renewal), plus expiry monitoring (90/60/30-day alerts) as the safety net. Machine certificates are infrastructure — their renewal must be as automatic as the WiFi they protect. The Saturday expiry was readable 3 years in advance; nobody read it
Issue 10-year certs to avoid this
Extend the expiry with a CA config change
Switch to password-based WiFi auth
scenarios.why: Certificate expiry is the most predictable outage in IT — the date is embedded in the certificate from issuance. Ten-year certs just schedule a bigger surprise later (and violate modern lifetime guidance). Issued certificates cannot be extended (the expiry is signed into them). Password WiFi is a security downgrade to dodge an operational failure. The correct system: certificates that renew themselves (auto-enrollment), monitored as a backstop (alerts at 90/60/30 days), with the renewal TESTED (a renewal that fails silently is the same outage, delayed). This applies to every machine-cert use: WiFi, VPN, ZTNA device identity. If your device trust depends on certificates, certificate lifecycle IS device-trust operations.
scenarios.hint: What are the two layers of certificate expiry defense?

scenarios.title: The TPM nobody uses
scenarios.situation: The fleet is 90% TPM 2.0-capable, BitLocker deployed. But device-trust policy does not check TPM attestation — 'we have BitLocker, that is enough.' A stolen laptop's BitLocker PIN is shoulder-surfed.
scenarios.prompt: What additional assurance does attestation provide?
evidence: TPM present, BitLocker on, but access policy ignores attestation. PIN compromise = full device trust.
The policy cannot distinguish 'genuine untampered device' from 'device with compromised boot chain.'
choices: Hardware-rooted boot integrity: TPM attestation lets the access policy verify the device BOOTED cleanly (measured boot — firmware, bootloader, OS hashes match known-good). BitLocker protects data at rest; attestation protects the TRUST decision — a device with a rootkitted boot chain fails attestation even with the right PIN. The stolen laptop with a tampered boot would fail closed instead of getting full access
BitLocker is sufficient; the PIN compromise is a user problem
TPM attestation is too complex to deploy
Require longer PINs instead
scenarios.why: BitLocker and attestation answer different questions: BitLocker asks 'is the disk encrypted?' (data at rest); attestation asks 'did THIS device boot the EXPECTED software?' (platform integrity). A shoulder-surfed PIN defeats the former; only the latter catches a tampered boot chain (evil-maid with modified bootloader still needs the PIN — attestation would flag the modified bootloader). 'Too complex' is a phasing argument, not a rejection (start with privileged devices). Longer PINs do not detect tampering. The hardware is already deployed and paid for — the policy just ignores it. For high-sensitivity access, 'TPM-attested boot' is the strongest device signal available; leaving it unused while buying more software controls is spending in the wrong place.
scenarios.hint: What question does attestation answer that BitLocker does not?

scenarios.title: The 30% unenrolled
scenarios.situation: MDM enrollment covers 70% of the laptop fleet. The other 30% are 'exceptions' — execs, lab machines, contractors — with full network access and no posture checks.
evidence: The exceptions are the HIGHEST-value targets (execs) and highest-risk (contractors).
choices: The exceptions ARE the attack surface: 30% of devices with zero posture signals and full access — inversely correlated with risk (execs targeted most, contractors least controlled). Fix: enroll or tier — every device gets a tier (managed / BYOD-registered / unknown), and access follows the tier. 'Exception' must mean 'different controls,' not 'no controls.' The 30% cannot keep full trust with zero verification
30% is acceptable; focus on the 70%
Force-enroll everyone Monday; exceptions are over
The execs will not tolerate MDM; leave them
scenarios.why: A 30% blind spot is not a rounding error — it is nearly a third of the fleet, and its composition (execs + contractors + lab oddities) is the worst possible selection: maximum target value, minimum control. 'Focus on the 70%' defends the already-defended. Forced Monday enrollment without a tier plan creates revolt (and the execs will win the exemption back). Leaving execs exempt formalizes 'the most targeted users have the least protection.' The workable path: tiered trust (managed = full, registered BYOD = constrained, unknown = portal-only), a real exception PROCESS (named owner, compensating controls, expiry — not vibes), and executive sponsorship that starts with the executives enrolling first. Coverage percentage is a security metric; drive it up deliberately.
scenarios.hint: What should 'exception' mean in a device program?

scenarios.title: The smart TV on the corporate LAN
scenarios.situation: A pentest finds 40 IoT devices (smart TVs, printers, HVAC controllers) on the corporate LAN with full peer connectivity — one compromised TV was used as a pivot in the test.
scenarios.prompt: What is the IoT segmentation answer?
evidence: 40 IoT, unmanageable agents, rare patches, full LAN access.
TV compromised → scanned the LAN → reached a file server. Flat network, no barriers.
choices: Dedicated IoT segment with default-deny: IoT devices cannot run agents or take posture checks, so they get network-level containment — their own VLAN/segment, internet-only (or vendor-cloud-only) access, NO path to user/server segments, and monitoring for anomalous traffic (a TV talking to the file server is an alert). The TV cannot be trusted, so it is contained
Install EDR on the TVs
IoT devices are low risk; document and accept
Put them on the guest WiFi
scenarios.why: IoT devices are unsecurable endpoints: no agents, infrequent patches, hardcoded credentials, decade-long lifespans. EDR is not installable. 'Low risk' ignores the pentest (the TV pivoted to a file server — the risk is demonstrated, not theoretical). Guest WiFi is closer but still shared with visitors and often routed permissively. The correct pattern: assume IoT is hostile (or soon will be), give it the minimum network it needs (usually vendor cloud + nothing else), deny everything else by default, and monitor for deviation (IoT traffic patterns are highly predictable — deviation IS the alert). Segmentation is the ONLY control for devices you cannot manage. Inventory them all; the 40 found are the ones the pentest noticed.
scenarios.hint: Why is segmentation the primary IoT control?

domains.name: Microsegmentation
domains.summary: Shrinking implicit trust zones: host firewalls, network segmentation, and workload isolation.

scenarios.title: The ransomware walk
scenarios.situation: Ransomware detonates on one workstation. Within 40 minutes it has encrypted 60 servers — the network is flat, one VLAN, no internal firewalling. The EDR caught the initial binary but not the lateral movement.
evidence: Single flat VLAN; any-to-any connectivity; no host firewalls (disabled 'for performance').
SMB lateral movement, 60 servers in 40 minutes. EDR saw the first host only.
choices: Microsegmentation: with workload-level (or at least tier-level) segmentation and default-deny, the ransomware's lateral movement hits walls — the workstation cannot reach servers' SMB, servers cannot reach each other laterally. EDR is detection; segmentation is CONTAINMENT. The 40-minute walk is the price of the flat network — assume breach means engineering the blast radius, not just detecting the breach
Better EDR would have stopped it
The firewall at the edge should have blocked it
Users need more phishing training
scenarios.why: EDR detected the detonation but lateral movement is a NETWORK problem: once the first host fell, SMB to 60 servers was permitted by the flat architecture. A better EDR might catch more, but detection is not containment — the tenet is assume breach, which demands the network resist a compromised host. The edge firewall never sees east-west traffic (the ransomware never left the LAN). Training reduces initial clicks; it does not contain the click that succeeds. Microsegmentation — even coarse tiering with host firewalls — converts '60 servers in 40 minutes' into '1 workstation, contained.' The lesson: detection tells you WHERE; segmentation decides HOW FAR. You need both, and the flat network had neither beyond the endpoint.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between detection and containment in this incident?

scenarios.title: The segmentation outage
scenarios.situation: Friday 6 PM: microsegmentation policy enforced on the app tier. Saturday: the batch jobs fail — they use a legacy port nobody documented. The policy was written from the CMDB, not from flow logs.
evidence: Written from CMDB documentation (stale); no flow discovery; enforced directly, no monitor mode.
Undocumented legacy port blocked; batch jobs (weekend-critical) down 14 hours.
choices: Flow discovery and monitor-mode: the policy lifecycle is discover (flow logs) → model → monitor-mode (log would-deny) → enforce — the team skipped to enforce from documentation. CMDBs describe intended architecture; flow logs describe REALITY. The 14-hour outage was the discovery phase happening in production. Roll back to monitor mode, collect flows, fix the policy, then re-enforce
The batch jobs should use standard ports
Segmentation is too risky; roll it back permanently
The CMDB needs updating
scenarios.why: Documentation describes the network as designed; flow logs describe the network as BUILT — and the gap is where outages live. The legacy port was real traffic the CMDB forgot. Monitor-mode exists precisely for this: it would have logged the would-deny for the batch port during the week, and Friday's enforcement would have included it. 'Use standard ports' does not fix the deployed reality. Rolling back permanently surrenders the security goal to one bad rollout. Updating the CMDB is good hygiene but does not replace flow-based discovery (the CMDB will drift again). The lifecycle order is non-negotiable: discover from reality, model, monitor, THEN enforce. Every segmentation outage is a skipped step made visible.
scenarios.hint: Why must segmentation policy come from flow logs, not documentation?

scenarios.title: The iLO on the user LAN
scenarios.situation: A pentest accesses an iLO management interface from the user LAN (default credentials) and mounts a virtual ISO to a production hypervisor host.
evidence: BMC/iLO/iDRAC interfaces on the user LAN, default creds, no network isolation.
Full host control via virtual media — below the hypervisor, invisible to EDR.
choices: Management-plane isolation FIRST: admin interfaces (BMC, iLO, switch management, hypervisor management) belong on a dedicated management segment reachable only from admin workstations/jump hosts — with non-default credentials. The management plane is the keys to everything; it is segmentation priority #1 because its compromise bypasses every higher-layer control (the attacker is BELOW the OS)
Change the default credentials; that is enough
iLO needs to be accessible for remote admins
The pentest was unrealistic; attackers do not do this
scenarios.why: Default credentials are one finding; LAN-reachable BMCs are the architectural one. Even with strong passwords, the management interface on the user LAN is one vulnerability away from host takeover — and host takeover defeats EDR, logging, and every guest-level control simultaneously (the attacker is beneath them all). Remote admin access is served by the isolated management segment + jump host, not by LAN exposure. 'Unrealistic' ignores that BMC exploitation is a standard pentest AND real-attacker technique (it is quiet, powerful, and rarely monitored). The priority order: management plane first (highest leverage, lowest app risk — nothing user-facing breaks), then server tiers, then users. Segment the keys before the rooms.
scenarios.hint: Why is management-plane segmentation priority #1?

scenarios.title: The blind east-west
scenarios.situation: The SOC has full north-south visibility (edge firewall, proxy logs) but zero east-west: when a server starts scanning the data tier, nobody sees it until the ransom note.
evidence: North-south: excellent. East-west: nothing — no flow logs, no IDS between segments, no host firewall deny logging.
Lives east-west by design (lateral movement never crosses the edge).
choices: East-west visibility: attackers operate server-to-server, deliberately avoiding the monitored edge. Deploy flow logging (VPC flow logs, NetFlow, host firewall deny logs) between segments, IDS on inter-tier paths, and alert on anomalous east-west patterns (a web server scanning the DB tier is never normal). The edge is the wrong place to watch for lateral movement — instrument where the attacker walks
The edge firewall needs better rules
More proxy logging will cover it
East-west monitoring is too expensive
scenarios.why: The monitored edge watches the door; the attacker is already inside walking the hallways. Every lateral-movement technique (SMB scanning, RDP hopping, credential replay) is east-west by nature — north-south controls are structurally blind to it. Better edge rules do not see internal traffic. Proxy logs cover user web traffic, not server-to-server. 'Too expensive' misprices it: flow logs are among the cheapest telemetry per insight (and cloud-native flow logging is nearly free to enable). The microsegmentation program and the visibility program are twins — the same flow data that WRITES the policy also DETECTS its violation. Deploy them together: segment the tiers, log the flows, alert on the anomalies.
scenarios.hint: Why is north-south monitoring blind to lateral movement?

scenarios.title: The five-year-old allow
scenarios.situation: Firewall review finds 300 allow rules; 120 reference decommissioned servers, 40 allow 'temporary' access from 2019. Nobody owns them. A pentest pivots through a 2019 'temporary' rule.
evidence: 300 allows, ~50% stale, zero owners, zero review history.
2019 temporary rule → decommissioned server IP (reassigned to a new VM) → pivot path.
choices: Rule lifecycle with ownership and expiry: every allow gets an owner, a reason, and a review/expiry date; quarterly reviews prune the dead; 'temporary' rules get 30-day expiries enforced by automation. The 2019 rule survived because nothing ever asked 'is this still needed?' Stale allows are not neutral — IP reuse turns dead rules into live holes
Delete all the rules and start over
The IP reassignment process is at fault
300 rules is too many; consolidate
scenarios.why: Firewall rules are access grants with the same lifecycle needs as any grant: owner, justification, expiry, review. Without it, entropy wins — 'temporary' becomes permanent, decommissioned servers' rules linger, and IP reassignment reactivates dead paths (the 2019 rule pointed at an IP that now belongs to something else). Deleting everything is a production outage. IP reassignment is normal operations; the rule should have died with the server. Consolidation without lifecycle just makes fewer, still-stale rules. The fix: rule-as-code (every rule in git with owner + reason + expiry), automated expiry enforcement, quarterly attestation ('I still need these N rules'), and a decommission checklist that includes firewall rules. Stale access is the commonest vulnerability class — in firewalls as in IAM.
scenarios.hint: Why do stale firewall rules become MORE dangerous over time?

scenarios.title: The mesh without policy
scenarios.situation: The team deploys a service mesh: mTLS everywhere between 200 microservices. But no authorization policies are configured — any authenticated service can call any other. A compromised logging sidecar queries the payments database service.
scenarios.prompt: What half of the mesh is missing?
evidence: mTLS: yes (encrypted, authenticated). Authorization: none (default allow).
Compromised low-value service reaches the highest-value service — encryption did not stop it.
choices: Authorization policy (default-deny): mTLS proves WHO is calling, but without authorization policy any authenticated identity can call anything — the mesh encrypted the attack path. The missing half is per-service allow-lists (payments accepts only from orders on /charge), ideally L7. Encryption without authorization is a faster, quieter breach
mTLS is misconfigured; fix the certificates
The logging sidecar should not have a cert
200 microservices is too many; consolidate
scenarios.why: The mesh has two security properties and the team deployed one: mTLS gives confidentiality + authentication (WHO is calling, encrypted), authorization policy gives the decision (MAY they call). Without the second, the mesh is an encrypted flat network — the compromised sidecar's calls are authenticated, encrypted, and completely unauthorized, which describes the incident exactly. Certificate fixes do not add authorization. Denying the sidecar a cert is whack-a-mole (the next compromised service has one). Consolidation does not fix the missing control. The rule: deploy mTLS AND default-deny authorization together, or do not claim the mesh's security value. 'Encrypted' is not 'authorized' — teach the distinction until it sticks.
scenarios.hint: What are the mesh's two security properties, and which was missing?

scenarios.title: The 0.0.0.0/0 security group
scenarios.situation: Audit finds a cloud security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0 to port 22 on 30 database servers — 'temporary for the migration,' 8 months ago. The migration ended in March.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cloud microsegmentation failure?
evidence: 0.0.0.0/0:22 on DB tier, labeled temporary, 8 months old.
SSH open to the internet on the data tier — brute-forced daily per logs.
choices: Temporary rules without expiry + no review: the cloud equivalent of the firewall rot — 'temporary' with no enforcement becomes permanent, and 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH is an internet-facing data tier. Fix immediately (scope to the bastion/jump host security group), then: security-group rules as code with expiries, quarterly reviews, and alerting on 0.0.0.0/0 to sensitive ports (it should page, not sit in a report)
Close port 22; nobody needs SSH
The migration team needed it; extend the exception
Cloud security groups are not real firewalls
scenarios.why: 0.0.0.0/0 to SSH on databases is about as exposed as infrastructure gets — and it sat for 8 months because 'temporary' had no machinery behind it. Closing 22 entirely breaks legitimate admin (the answer is scoping to the bastion, not removal). Extending the exception blesses the exposure. Security groups ARE the firewall in cloud — dismissing them is the old-network mindset. The cloud-native fix: infrastructure-as-code for security groups (every rule with owner/reason/expiry), automated expiry (the 'temporary' rule dies on schedule), and detective controls (config rules alerting on 0.0.0.0/0 to sensitive ports within minutes). Cloud speed means cloud rot accumulates faster — the lifecycle discipline must be automated, not manual.
scenarios.hint: How do you prevent 'temporary' cloud rules from becoming permanent?

domains.name: ZTA Migration Planning
domains.summary: Moving from perimeter security to zero trust: discovery, prioritization, pilots, and rollout strategy.

scenarios.title: The 18-month big bang
scenarios.situation: The CISO proposes an 18-month 'zero trust transformation': rip out VPN, re-architect network, deploy 5 new products, migrate all 400 apps — starting with the core network rebuild in month 1.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this plan?
evidence: Big-bang, 18 months, network-first, all apps, 5 products, no pilot, no wave metrics.
The last 18-month security program died at month 7 when the firewall migration broke payroll.
choices: Everything: big-bang plans die under their weight — no early wins to sustain funding, maximum blast radius on every change, and network-first means the hardest, riskiest work happens before any value is proven. The viable alternative: identity foundation first (weeks, visible), then a bounded pilot (one app, measured), then waves funded by results. The 18-month vision can exist — as a DIRECTION, not a project plan
18 months is too short; plan for 3 years
The product selection needs more evaluation first
Start with the network; it is the foundation
scenarios.why: Big-bang transformations fail for structural reasons: they concentrate risk (every change is load-bearing), delay value (nothing improves until month 18), and die on first contact with reality (the payroll outage at month 7). Longer timelines do not fix the structure. More product evaluation delays value further. Network-first puts the riskiest work (where outages live) before any credibility is earned. The alternative is not 'no plan' — it is wave-based: each wave is a funded, bounded, measured increment whose success funds the next. The 18-month DIRECTION guides wave selection; the WAVES are the plan. Programs survive on demonstrated value, not on architecture diagrams.
scenarios.hint: Why do big-bang security programs die?

scenarios.title: The wrong pilot
scenarios.situation: The team pilots ZTNA on the legacy trading application: thick client, custom protocol, 5 users, zero tolerance for downtime. The pilot struggles for 3 months, users hate it, and the steering committee questions the whole program.
scenarios.prompt: What was wrong with the pilot selection?
evidence: Hardest protocol, tiny user base, zero downtime tolerance, no rollback story.
3 months of struggle, hostile users, program credibility damaged.
choices: The pilot maximized difficulty and minimized learning value: pilots should be REPRESENTATIVE enough to learn from and FORGIVING enough to fail safely — a common web app with tolerant users (the CRM, 50 users) teaches the same lessons (identity, policy, UX, operations) at a fraction of the risk. Pilots pick wins, not heroics; the trading app is wave 3 material, after the patterns are proven
The team lacked skills; hire ZTNA experts
The product cannot handle thick clients; switch products
Pilots are a waste; go straight to production
scenarios.why: Pilot selection determines whether the program lives: a struggling pilot does not teach 'ZTNA is hard' — it teaches the steering committee 'this program fails.' The trading app combined every difficulty (custom protocol, zero tolerance, tiny sample) while teaching nothing a CRM pilot would not have taught about identity, policy design, UX, and operations. Skills and products were not the problem; the problem was sequencing. The rule: pilot the COMMON case first (web apps, tolerant users, visible win), expand to the hard cases with proven patterns. Save heroics for wave 3, when the team has scars and the committee has confidence. A pilot is a credibility engine — fuel it with wins.
scenarios.hint: What makes a good pilot selection?

scenarios.title: The forgotten mainframe
scenarios.situation: The migration plan covers 395 of 400 apps. The 5 unmentioned: the mainframe terminal emulator, the badge system, the HVAC controller, and 2 lab instruments. The breach comes through the badge system.
scenarios.prompt: What planning gap did the breach exploit?
evidence: 400 apps inventoried, 395 planned, 5 'out of scope' with no documentation.
Badge system (unpatched, flat network, default creds) → pivot → file server.
choices: The unplanned tail: every 'out of scope' system needs a NAMED disposition — migrate, isolate with compensating controls, or formally risk-accept with an owner and expiry. 'Out of scope' without documentation is not scoping; it is forgetting. The badge system needed a segment, a jump host, credential rotation, and monitoring — the standard exception package. Attackers inventory your network better than your plan did
The badge vendor is at fault
400 apps is too many; reduce scope
Badge systems cannot be secured
scenarios.why: Scope boundaries are legitimate — undocumented ones are just gaps. The 5 unmentioned systems were not 'out of scope'; they were unexamined, which is why the badge system sat unpatched with default credentials on the flat network. Vendor blame does not fix the architecture. Reducing scope does not help (the 5 were already 'out'). 'Cannot be secured' is false — they get compensating controls (isolation, jump hosts, monitoring), the standard package for un-migratable systems.
