The discipline: the inventory's last column is 'disposition' for EVERY row — migrate (which wave), contain (which controls), or accept (whose signature, what expiry). No blank cells. Attackers do not respect your scope document; they read the network.
scenarios.hint: What disposition must every inventoried system receive?

scenarios.title: The wave with no exit
scenarios.situation: Wave 1 'completes' — the team declares success because the tasks are done. But VPN usage is unchanged (users kept both), auth tickets rose (friction), and nobody measured phishing outcomes. Wave 2 funding is questioned.
evidence: Tasks done: SSO deployed, ZTNA piloted on 2 apps.
VPN unchanged, tickets up, security outcomes unmeasured. No exit criteria were defined.
choices: Exit criteria defined BEFORE the wave: waves end on OUTCOMES, not task completion — e.g., 'VPN sessions for pilot apps down 70%, auth tickets neutral-or-better, user satisfaction >4/5.' Task-complete without outcome-change is activity, not progress. The unchanged VPN usage reveals the real failure: users were never migrated OFF the old path (no sunset, no incentive). Wave 2's funding question is the bill for wave 1's missing metrics
The team needs more time; extend wave 1
Users are resistant; mandate ZTNA use
The metrics do not matter; the architecture is right
scenarios.why: Task completion is the wrong finish line: the wave's purpose was changing security outcomes (less VPN dependence, better auth, less friction), and none moved. Mandating use without fixing friction breeds workarounds. More time on undefined goals produces more undefined results. 'Architecture is right' is irrelevant if nobody uses it — adoption IS the architecture's success metric. The fix is procedural: every wave charter states exit criteria as measurable outcomes, with baselines captured before the wave starts. And migration requires decommissioning the old path — running old and new in parallel indefinitely doubles cost and halves the security gain. Users kept the VPN because nothing asked them not to. Define done as DONE (old path gone), in numbers, before starting.
scenarios.hint: Why must waves end on outcomes, not task completion?

scenarios.title: The budget that ran out
scenarios.situation: Year 1 funding covered the ZTNA purchase and deployment. Year 2 budget: zero — 'the project is done.' The licenses renew in 3 months, the contractor who ran it left, and no one owns the policy updates.
evidence: Deployed but unfunded: licenses lapsing, expertise gone, policies fossilizing.
Funded as a PROJECT (one-time) instead of a PROGRAM (ongoing).
choices: Zero trust needs program funding: licenses renew, policies need tuning, staff need retaining, the threat landscape moves. The year-1 business case should have shown year 2+ operating costs and the metrics justifying them (incident reduction, audit savings, productivity). 'Project is done' misunderstands the deliverable — the deliverable is an OPERATING capability, not a deployment. Emergency fix: bridge funding tied to the outcome metrics; structural fix: permanent ownership + operating budget + roadmap
The vendor should include lifetime licenses
Cut the ZTNA and go back to VPN; it was cheaper
The contractor should have documented better
scenarios.why: Security capabilities are not appliances you buy once: they are living systems needing licenses, people, and tuning. Funding the deployment without the operation is building a car with no fuel budget — it runs until the tank empties, then it is a monument. Reverting to VPN destroys the investment and the security gains. Documentation does not replace ownership (someone must DO the tuning). Vendor lifetime licenses do not exist for enterprise software. The governance fix: business cases state total cost of ownership (years 1–3+), metrics prove ongoing value (the monthly one-pager), and ownership is a named role with budget — not a contractor who leaves. Programs that cannot show year-2 value do not deserve year-2 funding; programs that CAN should never have to beg for it. Build the value case from wave 1.
scenarios.hint: Why must zero trust be funded as a program, not a project?

scenarios.title: The friction revolt
scenarios.situation: The ZTNA rollout requires MFA re-prompt every 30 minutes and blocks copy-paste in the VDI. Users revolt: 200 tickets in a week, executives demand exemptions, and shadow IT (personal Dropbox) spikes.
evidence: 30-min re-auth, no clipboard, no downloads — maximum friction, applied uniformly.
Ticket storm, executive exemptions (the worst precedent), shadow IT growth (the actual security loss).
choices: Security-usability balance, calibrated by risk: 30-minute re-auth for the intern portal is pointless friction; clipboard blocks for all apps equally is lazy policy. Calibrate: high-friction controls for high-sensitivity apps, streamlined for low-risk — and MEASURE friction (tickets per 1000 logins, satisfaction) alongside security. The shadow-IT spike is the real damage: users bypassed the controls entirely, ending LESS secure than before. Friction that drives circumvention is negative security
Users must accept the friction; security comes first
Roll back all the controls
Exempt the executives; they are busy
scenarios.why: 'Security comes first' ignores that bypassed security protects nothing — the personal-Dropbox spike means sensitive data now lives entirely outside every control. Rolling back everything surrenders the gains. Executive exemptions create the two-tier precedent that kills programs (and exempts the most-targeted users). The professional answer is calibration: risk-based friction (tight for the ERP, light for the wiki), measured continuously (friction metrics are program metrics), with user feedback loops (the ticket spike was DATA — the policy was wrong, not the users). Zero trust that users hate becomes zero trust that users evade. Design for the humans you have: make the secure path the EASY path, and reserve friction for where the risk justifies it.
scenarios.hint: Why is user circumvention a security metric?

scenarios.title: The app nobody inventoried
scenarios.situation: Six months into migration, the team discovers the customer-support team built a whole workflow on an unsanctioned SaaS tool (with customer data, SSO-less, paid on a corporate card). It is now business-critical and cannot simply be shut off.
evidence: Unsanctioned SaaS, customer data, no SSO, no DLP, now critical.
No CASB, no SaaS-spend analysis, no network-based discovery — the inventory was 'ask each department,' which missed it.
choices: Continuous SaaS discovery: CASB / SSE discovery, corporate-card spend analysis, DNS/proxy log analysis for unknown SaaS domains — 'ask around' is not discovery. Then the triage: bring it into the identity perimeter (SSO, DLP, policy) or provide a sanctioned alternative and migrate. Shutting it off outright breaks the business unit that depends on it (they will just find another shadow tool). The embarrassment is not that it exists — it is that discovery took 6 months
Block the SaaS domain immediately
Punish the support team for violating policy
Shadow IT is unstoppable; ignore it
scenarios.why: Blocking breaks a business-critical workflow overnight — the team will route around you by Friday. Punishment teaches concealment, not compliance (the next tool will be better hidden). Ignoring it leaves customer data outside every control indefinitely. Shadow IT exists because sanctioned IT was too slow or too rigid — treat it as a requirements signal, not just a violation. The mature response: discover continuously (automated, not surveys), triage quickly (sanction-and-secure vs replace-and-migrate), and fix the intake process so the NEXT team gets a fast sanctioned path instead of going rogue. Every shadow tool is a vote of no confidence in IT's responsiveness — count the votes and respond.
scenarios.hint: What does shadow IT indicate about IT's service, and how should you respond?

domains.name: ZTNA Architecture
domains.summary: Zero trust network access: replacing VPN with identity-aware, per-application access.

scenarios.title: The ZTNA purchase without identity
scenarios.situation: The company buys a ZTNA product and deploys it — on top of password-only authentication, no device checks, flat policies ('allow all employees to all apps'). The CISO presents it as 'zero trust achieved.'
evidence: ZTNA broker live; auth: AD passwords; device: unchecked; policy: one allow-all rule.
'Zero trust achieved' — the architecture says otherwise.
choices: Everything the tenets require: ZTNA is an enforcement mechanism, not the architecture — without strong identity (MFA, phishing-resistant for privileged), device signals, and per-app least-privilege policy, it is a VPN with a modern broker (same trust model: authenticate once, reach far). The purchase was step 4 of the playbook executed as step 1. Fix: identity foundation, device compliance, policy per app — THEN the broker enforces something meaningful
The product is misconfigured; tune it
A different ZTNA vendor would include identity
Zero trust is achieved; the CISO is right
scenarios.why: ZTNA answers 'HOW does the user reach the app?' — it does not answer 'HOW do we know it is really them, on a safe device, for an appropriate session?' Those answers are identity, device trust, and policy — the layers the deployment skipped. An allow-all policy through a ZTNA broker grants the same broad access the VPN did; the attacker with a password gets everywhere, just via a nicer portal. No vendor bundles 'your identity program' — that is organizational work. Tuning cannot create missing foundations. The sequencing matters: identity → device → policy → enforcement. Buying the enforcement first is building the roof before the walls. Call it phase 1 of 4, not 'achieved.'
scenarios.hint: Why is ZTNA without strong identity just a prettier VPN?

scenarios.title: The single connector
scenarios.situation: The ZTNA private-access connector runs on one VM ('we will add HA later'). It crashes Saturday. All internal app access dies — 500 users cannot work Monday until it is rebuilt.
evidence: Single VM, no HA, no monitoring. Critical path for all private access.
One VM failure = total internal-app outage. Rebuild took 6 hours.
choices: The connector is critical-path infrastructure: it gets HA (N+1 connectors, load-balanced), monitoring (health checks, session counts, alerting), and documented recovery from day one — 'later' never comes until the outage. The ZTNA fabric moved the single point of failure from the VPN concentrator to the connector; the architecture must treat it with the same seriousness (redundant, monitored, tested failover)
Connectors are unreliable; use VPN instead
One VM is fine with good backups
The outage was bad luck
scenarios.why: Every remote-access architecture has a critical path — the design question is whether it is redundant and monitored. A single connector is a single point of failure by construction; its crash was not bad luck but the expected outcome of a known SPOF. Backups shorten rebuilds but do not prevent the outage (6 hours is still 6 hours). VPN has the same property (concentrator clusters exist for this reason) — switching back does not fix the thinking. The rule: any component whose failure stops work gets HA + monitoring + tested failover BEFORE production traffic. 'Later' is where SPOFs hide. The connector is infrastructure now — operate it like infrastructure.
scenarios.hint: What makes a component 'critical path,' and what does that demand?

scenarios.title: The name that would not resolve
scenarios.situation: ZTNA pilot: the app is reachable via broker, but users' browsers cannot resolve the internal hostname — it only exists in internal DNS, and the ZTNA client was not configured for split DNS. The pilot 'fails' for 2 weeks over a DNS setting.
scenarios.prompt: What was missed in the pilot design?
evidence: App up, broker up, but names do not resolve for ZTNA users.
Split-DNS / DNS-forwarding through the ZTNA path never configured or tested.
choices: The DNS plan: private access requires deciding which names resolve through the ZTNA path (internal zones via the connector/broker) vs locally — and TESTING it before users arrive. Name resolution is the #1 'mysterious' private-access failure because everything else can be green while DNS is wrong. The 2-week 'failure' was a 10-minute config, undiscovered for lack of a pre-flight checklist (resolve the name THROUGH the ZTNA path, from a pilot client, before go-live)
The ZTNA product's DNS is broken
Use IP addresses instead of names
Internal DNS should be public
scenarios.why: DNS is the invisible dependency of every access path: the broker, the policy, and the app can all be perfect while the client stares at 'name not resolved.' Split-DNS design (which suffixes go through the ZTNA resolver) is a required pilot deliverable, not an afterthought. Product blame misses that DNS behavior is configuration, not a bug. IP addresses 'fix' it by destroying maintainability (and breaking TLS cert validation). Public internal DNS leaks your namespace. The pre-flight checklist for ANY private-access app: from a pilot client on the ZTNA path, resolve the name, reach the port, authenticate, and verify the policy decision — in that order. DNS first, always.
scenarios.hint: Why is DNS the #1 mysterious ZTNA failure?

scenarios.title: The thick client that almost worked
scenarios.situation: Wave 2 includes a thick-client ERP. The ZTNA broker 'supports' it per the datasheet. In testing: the client hardcodes an IP, uses a custom UDP protocol, and breaks on the broker's session timeouts. Go-live is in 2 weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong in wave planning?
evidence: Thick client, hardcoded IP, custom UDP, session-sensitive. Datasheet said 'supported.'
Discovered in testing, 2 weeks before go-live. No fallback plan.
choices: App readiness was assumed from the datasheet: ZTNA compatibility must be TESTED per app (protocol support, hardcoded addresses, session behavior, UDP handling) BEFORE wave commitments — datasheets describe the common case. The thick client needs either a validated path (agent-based with UDP support, tested), a re-architecture (web frontend), or an honest exception (stays on VPN with compensating controls). Two weeks is not enough to invent any of these; the wave plan must slip or the app must defer
The vendor lied; switch ZTNA products
Force the go-live; users will adapt
Thick clients cannot use ZTNA
scenarios.why: Datasheet 'support' means 'we have a feature for this category' — not 'your specific hardcoded-IP custom-UDP client works.' The gap between those is discovered only by testing YOUR app, which is why app readiness testing precedes wave planning, not the reverse. Forcing go-live ships a broken migration (and the credibility damage). Product-switching mid-wave resets the timeline. 'Cannot use ZTNA' is false in general but possibly true for THIS app — which is exactly what the exception path is for (documented, controlled, reviewed). The wave-planning rule: no app enters a wave until its access path is TESTED (not datasheeted). Waves are built from validated apps; the unvalidated wait.
scenarios.hint: Why must app readiness be tested, not datasheeted?

scenarios.title: The timeout that broke the workflow
scenarios.situation: The ZTNA policy sets a 1-hour session timeout for all apps. The finance team's month-end close involves a 3-hour continuous ERP session — it drops mid-close, twice, losing work. Finance demands an exemption from ZTNA.
scenarios.prompt: What is the policy design error?
evidence: Uniform 1-hour timeout, all apps, all users.
Legitimate long workflow broken; exemption demanded (which would gut the policy).
choices: Uniform timeouts ignore workflow reality: session lifetimes should be risk-calibrated — the ERP finance module during close gets a longer session (with step-up auth and session recording as compensating controls), while the wiki keeps 1 hour. The exemption demand is the symptom; the blunt policy is the disease. Design policies from actual workflows (ask finance about close week BEFORE setting timeouts), and build the legitimate long-session path INTO the policy
Finance gets an exemption; their work is special
Shorten it to 30 minutes for better security
The ERP should auto-save; it is an app problem
scenarios.why: Security policy that breaks legitimate work gets bypassed — the exemption demand proves it. But exempting finance (the highest-risk users, the most sensitive app) is the worst possible outcome. Shortening the timeout doubles down on the error. App auto-save is a separate issue (and would not fix the re-authentication friction). The correct design: risk-calibrated sessions (sensitivity × workflow reality), with compensating controls for the longer sessions (step-up at start, recording during, re-verification of device posture mid-session). Policy design starts from user workflows, not from a round number. 'One hour for everything' is not a policy — it is a default that nobody thought about. Think about it, per app, with the users who live in it.
scenarios.hint: How should session timeouts be set?

scenarios.title: The broker with no logs
scenarios.situation: A user's ZTNA session is hijacked (token theft). Investigation: the broker logs only 'session started/ended' — no per-request detail, no device posture at decision time, no policy version. The timeline cannot be reconstructed.
evidence: Session start/end only. Missing: auth details, device signals, policy decisions, per-request audit.
Cannot determine what the attacker accessed, with what signals, under which policy.
choices: Per-session, per-decision audit: every ZTNA session must log identity (and assurance level), device posture AT DECISION TIME, the policy (and version) that allowed it, and per-request/per-app access detail. The broker is a security enforcement point — its logs are the evidentiary record (tenet 7). 'Session started' is a heartbeat, not an audit trail. Fix the logging, then re-investigate what the retained data allows
The broker product is inadequate; replace it
Session hijacking is unstoppable; accept it
More verbose logging would hurt performance
scenarios.why: An enforcement point without decision-grade logging is a black box: you cannot investigate what you did not record, and the hijack investigation needed exactly the missing fields (which policy version allowed it? what device signals were evaluated? what did the session touch?). Product replacement is premature — check whether the logging exists but was never enabled/configured (common). 'Unstoppable' is false (token binding, short sessions, anomaly detection all help). Performance concerns are tunable (sample, tier, ship off-box — not 'do not log'). The standard: every access decision logs WHO (assurance), WHAT DEVICE (posture snapshot), WHICH POLICY (version), and WHAT RESULT — per session, retained per policy, shipped to the SIEM. Tenet 7 requires it; incidents demand it.
scenarios.hint: What must every ZTNA access decision log?

scenarios.title: The ZTNA without deprovisioning
scenarios.situation: ZTNA is live for 200 users. Offboarding still takes 3 days ('we disable AD Monday, the ZTNA admin does his part Wednesday'). A terminated employee accesses the CRM via ZTNA on Tuesday using a still-valid session token.
evidence: AD disabled Monday; ZTNA sessions/tokens live until Wednesday's manual cleanup.
Terminated user, valid ZTNA session, Tuesday access.
choices: Identity-lifecycle integration: IdP disable must propagate to the ZTNA fabric IMMEDIATELY — session/token revocation on identity disable, automated (SCIM/event-driven), not a Wednesday manual task. The 3-day gap is a standing ex-employee access window. Fix: wire IdP-disable → ZTNA revoke (test the kill chain latency), shorten token lifetimes so the worst case is minutes, and audit the propagation delay as a metric
Offboard faster; the process is just slow
The employee would not really do anything malicious
Disable ZTNA sessions nightly for everyone
scenarios.why: 'Faster' without automation is exhortation, not a fix — the manual Wednesday step will always lag. Trusting the terminated employee's goodwill is not a control. Nightly session kills punish every user for an integration gap. The missing piece is architectural: the ZTNA broker must subscribe to identity lifecycle events (disable → revoke NOW), because the broker mints the sessions and only the broker can kill them authoritatively. Test it: disable a test account, measure seconds until ZTNA sessions die — that latency is a security metric, publish it. Short token lifetimes bound the worst case even when integration hiccups. Deprovisioning is the identity perimeter's most important operation; the ZTNA fabric is inside that perimeter, not beside it.
scenarios.hint: Why must IdP-disable propagate to ZTNA automatically?

domains.name: Data-Centric Protection
domains.summary: Classifying data, encrypting flows, DLP, and protecting the resource itself rather than the network around it.

scenarios.title: The SSNs in the marketing share
scenarios.situation: DLP monitor mode finds 12,000 SSNs in the marketing file share — a legacy export from 2019 that nobody cleaned up. It is readable by 80 people, unencrypted, never accessed in 2 years.
evidence: 12k SSNs, stale, broadly shared, unencrypted. No business need identified.
Breach of that share = 12k identity-theft victims; the data serves no purpose.
choices: Remove it: stale sensitive data with no business need is pure liability — securely delete the export, verify no copies (backups included in scope), and find WHY it landed there (broken export process?) to prevent recurrence. Data minimization beats protection: the cheapest data to protect is data you do not have. Then scan for other stale exports
Encrypt the share; the data might be needed someday
Restrict the share to fewer people
It has been there 2 years safely; leave it
scenarios.why: 'Might be needed someday' is how 12k SSNs sit unencrypted for years — and 'safely' means 'not yet breached.' Encryption and tighter ACLs protect data that SHOULD exist; this data should not exist at all. Every stale sensitive copy is breach liability with zero business value. The correct hierarchy: (1) delete what has no purpose (minimization), (2) protect what remains (encryption, access control, DLP). Then fix the source: the 2019 export process that sprayed SSNs into a marketing share is the systemic bug — find it, fix the query, add DLP monitoring on the export path. Data you do not have cannot leak, cannot be stolen, and costs nothing to protect.
scenarios.hint: What is cheaper than protecting sensitive data?

scenarios.title: The PANs in the log
scenarios.situation: A developer debugging a payment issue logs full request bodies — including credit-card PANs — to the central log system. The logs are retained 90 days, readable by 200 engineers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the exposure and fix?
evidence: Full PANs in plaintext logs, 90-day retention, 200 readers, backed up, replicated.
Every logged transaction's PAN — PCI scope now includes the entire logging pipeline.
choices: Full log exposure: the PANs must be purged (and the logging fixed to mask/tokenize BEFORE writing), the log pipeline's PCI scope assessed (it is now in scope — expensive), and access reviewed. The developer's intent was fine; the practice violated the core rule — sensitive data NEVER in logs. Fix: mask at the logging call site (log tokens, never PANs), add log-scanning to CI (fail builds that log sensitive patterns), and treat the historical logs as compromised data requiring purge
The logs are internal; the risk is low
Delete the specific log lines; problem solved
Developers need full data to debug
scenarios.why: 'Internal' logs with 200 readers, backups, and 90-day retention are not a safe place for PANs — they are a distributed, durable copy of the card data, outside every PCI control. Deleting lines is whack-a-mole (backups, replicas, and the next developer's debug session). Developers need DEBUGGABILITY, not plaintext PANs — tokens correlate transactions without exposing cards. The systemic fixes: (1) mask/tokenize at the source (the logging statement), (2) CI gates that reject sensitive patterns in log statements, (3) periodic log scanning (the zt2 grep test, automated). And the compliance reality: the log pipeline just entered PCI scope — the QSA will want evidence of the purge and the preventive controls. One debug session's convenience created a 90-day, 200-reader exposure.
scenarios.hint: Why must sensitive data never reach logs, even 'temporarily'?

scenarios.title: The spreadsheet to Gmail
scenarios.situation: DLP blocks an employee emailing a customer list to their personal Gmail — 'I was going to work on it over the weekend.' The employee is angry; their manager asks for a DLP exception.
evidence: Blocked exfiltration of customer PII to personal email. Intent claimed benign.
Manager wants a standing exception for the team.
choices: No standing exception: the block WORKED — customer PII to personal Gmail is exfiltration regardless of intent, and 'weekend work' does not authorize it. Handle the legitimate need properly (secure remote access via ZTNA/VDI for weekend work — the data never leaves), investigate proportionally (was this a one-off or a pattern? check DLP history), and use it as a coaching moment. Granting the exception teaches that DLP is negotiable
Grant the exception; the intent was benign
Punish the employee severely as a deterrent
Disable DLP for managers' teams
scenarios.why: Intent does not change the data flow: customer PII in personal Gmail is outside every control (no DLP, no retention, no breach-notification capability, Google's subpoena target). Benign intent this time does not predict next time — and the DLP cannot distinguish them anyway. A standing exception for the team converts one blocked event into an open channel. Severe punishment for a first benign offense destroys the reporting culture (next time they will hide it better). The correct response addresses the NEED (weekend work) with a secure path (remote access where data stays in the perimeter) while holding the line on the CONTROL. And check the history — 'just this once' is verifiable. DLP exceptions are sometimes legitimate; 'email PII to personal accounts' is never one of them.
scenarios.hint: How do you handle the legitimate need behind a DLP block?

scenarios.title: The encrypted backups
scenarios.situation: Ransomware hits. The backup NAS — online, domain-joined — is encrypted too. The offline tape rotation was 'paused during the datacenter move' 4 months ago.
evidence: Online NAS encrypted with everything else. Offline rotation paused 4 months.
No recoverable copy. The ransom decision is now real.
choices: Backup isolation failure: the 3-2-1 rule requires an OFFLINE or IMMUTABLE copy — the online NAS was a second copy, not a backup (it shared the fate of the primary). 'Paused during the move' retired the only surviving layer for 4 months. Ransomware hunts backups first; the architecture must assume it. Rebuild: immutable object storage (object lock) + resumed offline rotation, with restores TESTED from the isolated copy
Pay the ransom; there is no alternative
The NAS vendor failed; replace it
Moves are risky; avoid datacenter moves
scenarios.why: A backup that shares the primary's fate is not a backup — it is a synchronized copy awaiting the same disaster. The 'pause' converted a 3-2-1 architecture into a 2-1-0 one for 4 months, precisely when the move (chaos, new network, distracted staff) raised the risk. Paying is sometimes the rational business call, but it is not the lesson — the lesson is architectural: immutability (even a compromised admin cannot delete object-locked backups) or air gaps (offline media the ransomware cannot reach), plus tested restores from the isolated copy. Vendor blame and move-avoidance miss the point. The question for every backup design: 'if the attacker owns the domain, which copy survives?' If the answer is 'none,' the design is wrong.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between a second copy and a backup?

scenarios.title: The analytics on plaintext
scenarios.situation: The analytics team queries production customer PII directly ('we need real data'). 30 analysts have read access to the full customer table including SSNs. Two analysts left last month; their access is still active.
evidence: 30 analysts, full PII, direct prod queries, 2 stale accounts.
Analytics on customer behavior — the SSN column is never used in their queries (verified).
choices: Data-centric minimization: the analysts do not need SSNs (verified unused) — tokenize or mask the sensitive columns in the analytics copy, give analysts the de-identified dataset, and keep the full PII behind the vault (detokenization only for the 2 fraud investigators with justification). Plus: kill the stale accounts immediately (the leaver gap again), and move analytics OFF production (replica/mart, not the live DB)
The analysts are trusted; the access is fine
Remove the 2 stale accounts; the rest is fine
Analytics needs prod; keep it as is
scenarios.why: Thirty people with SSN access they never use is thirty breach vectors for zero analytical value — the verified-unused finding is the key: it proves the access is unnecessary, which makes the fix painless (nobody's work changes). Tokenization/masking gives analysts everything they query while removing the sensitive columns from their blast radius. 'Trusted' is not a control (their accounts get phished like anyone's). Removing 2 stale accounts fixes 2 of 30 problems. Analytics on the live prod DB adds availability risk to the privacy risk. The data-centric principle: each consumer gets the MINIMUM fidelity they need — tokens for analytics, masked for support, full only for the vault-mediated few. Unused sensitive access is pure liability; the query logs prove it is unused, so remove it.
scenarios.hint: How do you prove sensitive access is unnecessary?

scenarios.title: The public bucket
scenarios.situation: A cloud storage bucket with customer documents is found publicly readable — misconfigured during a migration 5 months ago. Access logs show automated scanners hit it; no confirmed data theft, but it cannot be ruled out.
evidence: Public read, 5 months, customer documents. Scanner hits confirmed; exfiltration unconfirmable.
No bucket-policy monitoring, no public-access blocks at the account level.
choices: Treat as a breach: 5 months public with scanner hits means assume exposure — lock it down immediately (private + explicit deny), inventory what was in it, engage legal/IR for notification analysis (regulations care about EXPOSURE, not just confirmed theft), and fix the systemic gaps: account-level public-access blocks (prevent the class), config monitoring/alerting on public buckets (detect in minutes), and IaC for bucket policies (no click-ops drift)
No confirmed theft means no incident; just fix the config
Delete the bucket; the data is compromised anyway
It was only scanners; scanners do not steal data
scenarios.why: 'No confirmed theft' is not 'no theft' — 5 months of public exposure with scanner activity means the data must be assumed accessed (scanners enumerate; humans follow). Breach-notification laws trigger on unauthorized ACCESS/exposure, not on proven exfiltration — legal needs to evaluate from hour one. Deleting the bucket destroys evidence and the data (the business still needs the documents — secured). The systemic fixes are the real deliverable: account-level blocks make public buckets impossible by default (prevent), config rules alert within minutes (detect), IaC makes the policy reviewable (sustain). The migration created it; the missing guardrails let it live 5 months. Every cloud account needs the 'no public buckets' block as a baseline — it is one setting.
scenarios.hint: Why does unconfirmed exfiltration still trigger breach response?

scenarios.title: The TLS 1.0 in production
scenarios.situation: A scan finds TLS 1.0 still enabled on the customer portal 'for old client compatibility.' The portal handles logins and PII. PCI requires 1.2+.
evidence: TLS 1.0 enabled, production portal, PII in transit. PCI non-compliant.
choices: Disable it: TLS 1.0 is broken (BEAST et al.) and PCI-non-compliant — 'old clients' from 2018 is not evidence of current need. Quantify FIRST (what percentage of traffic is TLS 1.0-only? usually ~0%), notify if anyone real is affected, then disable and monitor. Compatibility with broken crypto is not compatibility — it is vulnerability. The 2018 rationale has not been re-examined in years
Keep it; breaking old clients is worse
Enable 1.3 alongside; the 1.0 will age out
It is only the portal; the API is modern
scenarios.why: TLS 1.0's weaknesses are not theoretical — they are practical, published, and PCI-forbidden. 'Old clients' is an unquantified ghost from 2018; measure it (the scan can show negotiated versions — it is almost always zero real users). Adding 1.3 does not remove 1.0's exposure (downgrade attacks target the weakest enabled version). 'Only the portal' is where the logins and PII are — the worst place for weak crypto. The pattern: legacy-compatibility exceptions need QUANTIFICATION and EXPIRY, not vibes from 2018. Measure, notify the (usually nonexistent) affected, disable, verify. Cryptographic agility means moving forward — every year you keep 1.0, the rationale gets weaker and the risk stays.
scenarios.hint: How do you retire a legacy crypto exception?

domains.name: Continuous Monitoring & Diagnostics
domains.summary: CDM, SIEM, behavioral analytics, and the feedback loop that makes trust decisions dynamic.

scenarios.title: The correlation that never fired
scenarios.situation: The SIEM ingests firewall logs only. An attacker's week: phished creds (IdP logs, not ingested) → lateral SMB (no east-west logging) → data staged (DLP not ingested) → exfiltrated via DNS (DNS logs not ingested). The firewall saw nothing anomalous.
scenarios.prompt: What is the SIEM coverage failure?
evidence: Firewall only. Missing: identity, EDR, DNS, DLP, cloud audit.
Lived entirely in the un-ingested layers — invisible by architecture.
choices: The SIEM watches one layer of a multi-layer attack: firewall-only ingestion is perimeter-era thinking. The fix is coverage by attack path — minimum viable: IdP/auth logs, EDR, DNS, firewall/PEP denies, cloud audit. Then detection engineering ON that data (the logs alone do not detect; correlations do). The attacker did not evade the SIEM; the SIEM was never pointed at them
The firewall needs better rules
Buy a better SIEM
The attack was too sophisticated to detect
scenarios.why: A SIEM is only as good as its inputs: with firewall-only ingestion, every attack that avoids the firewall (which is most modern attacks — they live in identity, endpoints, and DNS) is structurally invisible. Better firewall rules do not see EDR or IdP events. A better SIEM with the same inputs has the same blind spots. 'Too sophisticated' is false — each step was mundane and WOULD have been visible in the right log (impossible-travel in IdP, SMB scanning in EDR/flow logs, DNS tunneling in DNS logs). The coverage model: map your top attack paths, list the logs each step emits, ingest THOSE. Then write the correlations. SIEM value = coverage × detections; this deployment had neither.
scenarios.hint: What determines a SIEM's effective coverage?

scenarios.title: The 200-day dwell
scenarios.situation: Breach investigation: attacker present 200 days. The signs were in the logs (off-hours logons, new admin account created, large archive files). No one looked. MTTD is now a board-level question.
evidence: All logged, none alerted, none reviewed.
200 days — the attacker operated with impunity for over 6 months.
choices: Detection-process failure, not a tooling gap: the data existed; nobody converted it into detections, reviews, or alerts. Fix: the unholy trinity of 'always alert' — new privileged accounts, off-hours admin activity, and large outbound transfers — as SIEM rules THIS week; a weekly human review of high-risk alerts; and MTTD as a tracked metric with a target. The board question deserves a program answer, not a product purchase
Buy an AI-powered detection platform
200 days is industry average; it is fine
Hire more SOC analysts
scenarios.why: The logs contained the entire attack — the failure was 100% process: no detections for the obvious (new admin accounts should ALWAYS alert), no review cadence, no MTTD accountability. AI platforms do not fix missing fundamentals (and need tuning anyway). 'Industry average' is not a defense to the board (and averages are falling for shops that do the basics). More analysts without detections just scale the eyeballing of raw logs. The three rules (new priv accounts, off-hours admin, big egress) catch an enormous fraction of real intrusions and take a day to write. Then: weekly review ritual, MTTD tracked monthly, dwell-time goal published. Detection is a discipline with tool support — this shop had the tools and skipped the discipline.
scenarios.hint: What three detections should every SIEM have on day one?

scenarios.title: The UEBA that cried wolf
scenarios.situation: UEBA deployed in enforce mode day one. It flags the traveling sales team (new locations), the night-shift admins (off-hours), and the data scientists (large downloads) — 200 false positives in week one. The SOC disables it.
evidence: Enforce mode, day-one baselines (none), no tuning period.
False-positive storm → disabled → zero value, plus organizational scar tissue ('UEBA does not work').
choices: Skipping the baseline-and-tune phase: UEBA needs 2–4 weeks of learning before enforcement, starting in monitor mode, with the known-good weirdness (travelers, night shifts, data scientists) whitelisted BY PATTERN. Enforce-mode on day one guarantees the false-positive storm that gets it disabled. The scar tissue ('does not work') is now a bigger obstacle than the tuning would have been. Redeploy properly: monitor, tune, THEN enforce — and communicate the phases so the SOC expects the journey
UEBA does not work; remove it
The sales team should travel less
Tune it to be less sensitive permanently
scenarios.why: Behavioral analytics without baselines is just anomaly theater: every deviation from NOTHING is an alert. The deployment skipped the essential phases — learn (collect behavior), tune (encode the legitimate weirdness: sales travels, admins work nights, scientists download big), then enforce. Permanent desensitization trades false positives for false negatives (now it misses real attacks too). The organizational damage exceeds the technical: 'UEBA does not work' will block the next attempt. The redeploy must be explicitly phased and communicated: 'weeks 1–4: learning, expect noise, we are tuning; week 5+: enforcement begins.' Set expectations, tune visibly, enforce gradually. Detection systems are adopted, not just installed.
scenarios.hint: Why must UEBA start in monitor mode?

scenarios.title: The intel feed firehose
scenarios.situation: The team subscribes to 5 threat-intel feeds: 50,000 IOCs/day auto-ingested. The SOC ignores them (all noise, no context). A relevant ransomware IOC for their sector sat in the feed for 3 weeks, unactioned.
scenarios.prompt: What is the intel operationalization failure?
evidence: 5 firehoses, no filtering, no prioritization, no workflow.
Sector-relevant ransomware IOC unactioned for 3 weeks — it was in the noise.
choices: Curation and workflow, not volume: 50k IOCs/day is un-actionable by definition. Fix: filter to YOUR sector/stack/geography, prioritize (active exploitation + relevance), and build the intel-to-action workflow (auto-block high-confidence, hunt medium, ticket low) — with someone OWNING the feed. One curated feed with a workflow beats five firehoses with none. The ransomware IOC was 'in the feed' the way a needle is 'in the haystack'
Add more feeds for better coverage
Threat intel is overrated; drop it
The SOC should read all 50k daily
scenarios.why: Threat intel's value is entirely in operationalization: an IOC becomes valuable when it auto-blocks, triggers a hunt, or informs a decision — within hours, by a defined workflow. Fifty thousand unfiltered IOCs achieve none of that; they train the SOC to ignore the feed (rationally). More feeds multiply the noise. Dropping intel surrenders the early-warning value (the ransomware IOC WAS the warning, 3 weeks early). Nobody reads 50k IOCs. The mature model: few feeds, heavy filtering (sector + stack + active-exploitation), automated action tiers, named ownership, and metrics (IOCs actioned, hits found). Intel is a sensor — sensors need tuning and someone watching the output, or they are decoration.
scenarios.hint: What makes threat intel operational vs decorative?

scenarios.title: The red team that walked in
scenarios.situation: Annual pentest: testers phish one user, escalate to domain admin in 2 days, exfiltrate 'crown jewels' on day 4. Last year's test: nearly identical results. Nothing changed between tests.
evidence: Year 1 and Year 2: same path, same success, same report.
None of Year 1's findings were fixed — the test is a ritual, not a driver.
choices: Testing without remediation is theater: the pentest's value is entirely in the FIXES it drives. Findings need owners, deadlines, and verification (re-test the path next cycle — did the fix hold?). Year 2's identical results should have been a governance crisis, not a routine report. The assume-breach program REQUIRES this loop: test → fix → verify — the red team measures the architecture, but only remediation improves it
Hire better pentesters for new findings
Pentests are a compliance checkbox; this is normal
The testers should have tried harder paths
scenarios.why: A pentest that finds the same critical path two years running is not a testing failure — it is a REMEDIATION failure, and the more expensive one. New testers would find new paths while the old highway stays open. Checkbox-normal is exactly the disease (compliance satisfied, security unchanged). Harder paths miss the point: the EASY path still works. The fix is governance around findings: every critical finding gets an owner + deadline + retest; the steering committee reviews remediation rates (not just reports); repeat findings escalate (the same DA-escalation path twice is a leadership issue). Red-team results are the zero trust program's report card — but only if anyone reads the grades and does the homework. Test, fix, VERIFY. The verify step is where programs live or die.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between pentesting as ritual vs as a driver?

scenarios.title: The 100% MFA slide
scenarios.situation: The CISO's board slide: 'MFA enabled for 100% of users!' Reality: 80% SMS, 15% push, 5% FIDO2 — and the last breach was an MFA-fatigue push attack. The board thinks identity is solved.
scenarios.prompt: What is the metrics honesty failure?
evidence: Phishable methods dominate; the breach used the weakest enrolled method.
choices: Outcome metrics over checkbox metrics: report phishing-RESISTANT MFA rate (5% — the honest number), MFA-bypass incidents, and the migration plan to FIDO2. 'Enabled' measures deployment; 'phishing-resistant' measures SECURITY. The board was misled by a vanity metric into thinking a solved problem — metrics must reflect the threat model, not the project plan. Fix the metric, then fix the reality it reveals
The slide is accurate; 100% is 100%
Remove the MFA slide; metrics are political
Mandate FIDO2 overnight
scenarios.why: Vanity metrics are worse than no metrics: they create false confidence at the highest level ('identity is solved'), which starves the real fix of urgency and funding. '100% enabled' is deployment theater when 95% of it falls to push-bombing or SIM swap — the breach proved it. Dropping metrics abandons accountability. Overnight mandates break without provisioning and recovery processes. The honest metric — phishing-resistant MFA percentage, especially for privileged users — tells the true story (5%) and justifies the program (the FIDO2 rollout). Every security metric should be stress-tested against the question: 'if this number is high, are we actually safer?' If the answer is no, it is vanity. Report the number that hurts; then fix it.
scenarios.hint: What makes a security metric vanity vs honest?

scenarios.title: The logs that aged out
scenarios.situation: Incident response needs 8-month-old proxy logs. Retention is 90 days — the evidence is gone. The attacker was present for 7 months; the proof of initial access aged out.
evidence: 90 days, uniform, set years ago for storage costs.
7-month dwell needs 12+ months of key logs for investigation.
choices: Retention matched to threat reality: 90 days cannot investigate a 200-day dwell. Tier the retention — security-relevant logs (auth, proxy, DNS, EDR) 12+ months (hot 90d, warm/cold after), informed by YOUR dwell-time goals and regulatory needs. Storage cost is real, but so is investigation failure; tiered storage (hot/warm/cold) makes long retention affordable. The 90-day uniform policy was a cost decision masquerading as a design
Keep everything forever; storage is cheap
90 days is standard; the IR team should work faster
The attacker should have been caught in 90 days
scenarios.why: 'Should have been caught' does not recover the evidence — retention must handle the dwell times you actually have, not the ones you wish for. Forever-retention is unbounded cost with diminishing returns. The 90-day standard is a default, not a design (it predates your threat model). Tiered retention is the professional answer: hot storage for recent (fast queries), warm/cold for the long tail (cheap, slower) — 12–18 months for security logs is common and affordable in object storage. And the retention policy gets reviewed when dwell metrics change: if your MTTD is 200 days, 90-day retention guarantees evidence gaps. Design retention FROM the investigation need: 'we must be able to reconstruct the last N months' — then price the tiers. The evidence you need is always older than your retention.
scenarios.hint: How should log retention be designed?

domains.name: Governance, Risk & Compliance
domains.summary: Policy as code, audit evidence, regulatory mapping, and governing a zero trust program.

scenarios.title: The 2 AM firewall click
scenarios.situation: During an incident, an engineer opens a firewall rule via the cloud console 'temporarily.' 8 months later it is still there, undocumented, and a pentest uses it. No ticket, no review, no expiry.
scenarios.prompt: What process would have prevented this?
evidence: Click-ops, 2 AM, no record. Still live 8 months later.
Pentest pivot path — the 'temporary' rule, permanent.
choices: Policy-as-code with emergency workflow: the 2 AM change goes in as a PR (even retroactively within 24h) with reason + expiry; automation reverts expired rules; quarterly reviews catch the rest. Emergency changes are legitimate — undocumented permanent ones are not. The process must make the RIGHT thing the EASY thing: a one-command 'emergency grant with 24h expiry' beats a console click with no trail
Ban emergency changes; all changes need full review first
The engineer should be disciplined
Firewall rules do not need tracking
scenarios.why: Banning emergency changes guarantees they happen anyway, just secretly — incidents do not wait for change boards. Discipline does not scale; process does. 'No tracking needed' is how 8-month temporary rules happen. The mature pattern acknowledges reality: emergencies need FAST grants, so build the fast path WITH guardrails (pre-approved emergency workflow, automatic expiry, mandatory retroactive review within 24h). Policy-as-code makes this natural: the emergency PR is quick to write, the expiry is enforced by automation, and the review is a calendar event, not a hope. Every grant — especially the 2 AM ones — ends up owned, reasoned, and expirable. That is the whole game.
scenarios.hint: How do you handle emergency access grants without losing track?

scenarios.title: The annual audit fire drill
scenarios.situation: Every year, the SOC 2 audit triggers a 6-week scramble: screenshots, spreadsheets, and 'evidence' assembled from memory. The auditors get a curated story; the actual control state is unknown.
evidence: Annual 6-week evidence scramble, then 46 weeks of unknown state.
Controls drift between audits; the audit measures the scramble, not the year.
choices: Evidence as exhaust: with policy-as-code (every grant reviewed and logged), continuous monitoring (control state measured daily), and mapped artifacts (each control points at its evidence source), the audit becomes a report EXPORT — not a project. The 6-week scramble indicates controls are not continuously operated; fix the operation and the audit gets boring (boring audits are the goal)
Hire audit-prep consultants yearly
The scramble is normal; all companies do it
Reduce the audit scope
scenarios.why: The scramble is a symptom: if evidence takes 6 weeks to assemble, the controls were not being operated and measured continuously — the audit is sampling the scramble's output, not the year's reality. Consultants optimize the theater. 'Everyone does it' normalizes the dysfunction. Scope reduction dodges the question. Continuous compliance inverts the model: policy-as-code means every access change IS documented at change time; monitoring means control effectiveness is measured daily; the control-to-artifact map means the auditor's request resolves to existing reports. The audit then validates the system rather than inspiring a performance. Aim for the boring audit — it means the program runs itself.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between audit preparation and continuous compliance?

scenarios.title: The risk nobody owned
scenarios.situation: The risk register lists 'lateral movement via flat network' — owner: TBD, since 2021. The ransomware in 2024 used exactly that path. The register was reviewed never.
evidence: 2024: the registered risk materializes, exactly as described.
choices: Risk management as a living process: every risk gets an owner, a mitigation plan with dates, and a review cadence (monthly at steering). 'TBD' since 2021 means the register is a document, not a practice. The 2024 incident was FORECAST — the organization knew and did nothing, which is worse than not knowing (it is negligence with a paper trail). Fix: assign owners, fund mitigations, review monthly, and treat repeat-risk materialization as a governance crisis
Risk registers cannot prevent incidents
The 2021 assessment was wrong about likelihood
Remove the risk from the register; it already happened
scenarios.why: A risk register without owners and reviews is a prophecy archive: it predicts incidents without preventing them, then documents the negligence. 'Cannot prevent' is false — the register's PURPOSE is driving mitigation (the flat network was fixable in 2021–2024). The likelihood assessment was RIGHT (it happened). Removing it post-incident hides the governance failure. The living process: risks reviewed monthly, owners report mitigation progress, stale owners escalated, materialized risks trigger post-mortems on the GOVERNANCE (why did we know and not act?). The 2024 incident's most damning fact is not the ransomware — it is the 2021 register entry describing it. Governance exists to convert knowledge into action; this one converted it into paper.
scenarios.hint: What turns a risk register from prophecy into prevention?

scenarios.title: The mandate as leverage
scenarios.situation: The federal-adjacent agency must meet zero trust requirements (identity, device, network, app, data pillars) by the deadline. Leadership sees it as 'an IT compliance exercise.' The security team needs funding for the identity pillar.
scenarios.prompt: How should the mandate be used?
evidence: Binding requirements with a deadline, five pillars, measurable goals.
'IT compliance exercise' —最小 funded, minimal effort.
choices: The mandate is program leverage: translate pillar requirements into risk reduction and business terms ('the identity pillar closes the #1 breach path; non-compliance risks contract eligibility'), sequence the pillars by risk (identity first — it underpins the others), and use the deadline as the forcing function for decisions that otherwise drift. 'Compliance exercise' framing is fought with outcome metrics: show the mandate's goals reduce the incidents leadership already fears
Do the minimum to check the boxes
Mandates do not change anything; ignore the deadline
Hire lobbyists to extend the deadline
scenarios.why: Minimum-viable compliance wastes the mandate's forcing power: the deadline is the rare organizational asset that compels decisions, funding, and attention — spending it on checkbox theater squanders it. Ignoring it risks the mission (contract eligibility, audit findings). Lobbying the deadline is organizational learned helplessness. The strategic play: treat the mandate's pillars as the program's skeleton (they are a decent maturity model regardless of sector), fund them by risk priority, and report BOTH compliance progress and security outcomes — the mandate gets you in the door, the outcomes keep you funded after the deadline. Compliance deadlines are the security program's best friend: they convert 'someday' into 'by Q4.' Use them.
scenarios.hint: How do you turn a compliance mandate into security outcomes?

scenarios.title: The permanent temporary exception
scenarios.situation: The legacy VPN exception was granted 'temporarily' in 2021 for 20 users. It is now 2026: 200 users, no review ever, no owner (the sponsor left in 2022). It is the least-monitored access path in the company.
evidence: 2021 temporary, 200 users now, no owner, no review, minimal monitoring.
The exception became the norm — the least-controlled path, at scale.
choices: Exception lifecycle: every exception has an owner, a documented justification, compensating controls, a REVIEW DATE (max 1 year), and sunset criteria. At review: remediate, re-justify with fresh signatures, or revoke. The 2021 exception died with its sponsor because exceptions were not re-owned; the 10x user growth happened because nobody watched the scope. Fix now: assign an owner, assess the 200 users (who actually needs it?), apply controls, set the review date — and build the register so this cannot recur
Exceptions are necessary; leave it
Remove it immediately; exceptions are bad
The 200 users need it; formalize it as standard
scenarios.why: 'Necessary' does not mean 'unowned and unreviewed' — the exception's legitimacy in 2021 says nothing about 2026. Immediate removal without assessment breaks 200 users' work (and they will route around you). Formalizing it as standard blesses the least-controlled path as architecture. The discipline: exceptions are RENTED, not owned — rented with a lease (review date), rent paid in compensating controls, and the lease either renewed (re-justified, re-signed) or terminated. The register tracks every lease. Sponsor departure triggers re-assignment, not abandonment. Scope growth (20→200) triggers re-evaluation, not silent acceptance. 'Temporary' without machinery is permanent — build the machinery.
scenarios.hint: What is the lifecycle of a healthy exception?

scenarios.title: The architect who left
scenarios.situation: The zero trust architect — who designed everything, holds all the context, made all the decisions — resigns. The program stalls for 6 months. Nobody knows why the policies are shaped the way they are.
evidence: Single point of knowledge; decisions in one head; documentation sparse.
6-month stall; new architect reverses decisions without understanding them.
choices: Decision records and distributed ownership: architecture decision records (ADRs) for every major choice (what, why, alternatives rejected), policy-as-code (the policies ARE documented), runbooks for operations, and no single-owner components (every area has a primary AND a backup). The 6-month stall is the bill for hero-driven architecture. Programs must survive their champions — design for it from day one
Pay the architect more to stay
Hire a replacement quickly
The new architect should redesign from scratch
scenarios.why: Retention money delays the problem; it does not solve the single-point-of-knowledge design. Fast hiring does not transfer the departed context (the new hire inherits the mystery). Redesign-from-scratch discards working architecture out of ignorance — the reversals may reintroduce solved problems. The fix is structural and boring: ADRs (one page per major decision: context, options, choice, consequences), code-as-documentation (policy-as-code IS the policy spec), paired ownership (no area with one knower), and regular architecture reviews that spread context. Hero architects are a risk to be managed, not an asset to be celebrated — brilliance that cannot be inherited is technical debt with a resignation letter attached. Build the program so the bus factor is never 1.
scenarios.hint: How do you make a security program survive its architect?

scenarios.title: The five pillars, one funded
scenarios.situation: The program funds the network pillar (new firewalls, segmentation) heavily. Identity, device, app, and data pillars are unfunded — 'we will get to them.' The phishing-driven breach succeeds via credential theft on unmanaged devices.
evidence: Through the unfunded pillars — exactly where the money was not.
choices: Pillars are interdependent: network controls without identity and device signals are the old model with new paint — the breach walked through the gap between funded and unfunded. The pillar model exists to force BALANCED investment: identity first (it underpins every access decision), then devices, then network/app/data together. Rebalance: the next dollar goes to identity (phishing-resistant MFA) and device (compliance), because the breach named the priority
The network investment was wasted
More network spending will eventually cover it
Pillars are just a model; real security is holistic
scenarios.why: The network spend was not wasted — it was INSUFFICIENT ALONE, which is the pillar model's entire lesson: zero trust is five interdependent systems, and the program is only as strong as the weakest. Credential theft defeats network segmentation (the attacker authenticates, then walks through). 'More network' cannot fix an identity problem. 'Holistic' without the pillar discipline is how the 80/20 imbalance happened — vibes instead of allocation. The rebalancing rule: fund the pillar the last incident named, then the next-weakest, in rotation — and report maturity PER PILLAR so imbalances are visible to leadership. The model is a budgeting tool as much as an architecture: it makes underinvestment undeniable. Use it that way.
scenarios.hint: Why must pillar investment be balanced?

lessons.title: IL-11 Zero Trust & Endpoint Defense — Core concepts
concepts: Never trust, always verify (NIST SP 800-207): every access request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted based on identity, device posture, and context — per session, per resource. Network location ('inside the VPN') is context, never a grant of trust.

Identity is the perimeter: users, workloads, and devices each get strong, phishing-resistant identity, and access policies evaluate all three. Credentials answer 'who claims to be asking'; the policy must also ask 'on what device, in what state.'

Microsegmentation shrinks implicit trust zones to the smallest practical scope — ideally per workload — with default-deny between zones. It is blast-radius engineering: assume breach, then make sure the breach cannot walk laterally.

Endpoints are the battlefield: EDR/EPP provides the detection and response sensors that 'assume breach' depends on. Alert fidelity beats alert volume — untuned detections train analysts to bulk-close, which is how real precursors hide in noise.

Least privilege is temporal as well as scoped: standing admin rights (especially service accounts) are pre-authorized breach material. Prefer just-in-time, short-lived, narrowly-scoped credentials issued per task and revoked after.

Continuous verification replaces point-in-time checks: posture, behavior, and risk are re-evaluated through the session, and access adapts or revokes as signals change. Zero trust is a control loop, not a gate — which is why it is cybernetics applied to security.

example.code:
grep -Ei 'allow.*any.*any|permit.*0\.0\.0\.0' firewall.rules | head -20
# Any hit is a candidate over-broad rule: document it,
# then check whether a narrower source/destination/port tuple suffices.
example.walkthrough: Hunting 'allow any-any' rules is the fastest zero-trust audit: each hit is implicit trust granted to the whole network. The fix pattern is always the same — replace the broad rule with the narrowest tuple the workload actually needs.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating the VPN as zero trust — a VPN moves the perimeter to the user's device; it does not verify per-request, per-resource, or continuously.
Common trap: buying EDR and skipping tuning — default detections in your environment are noise generators; fidelity comes from baselining and allowlisting your own admin tooling.
Common trap: segmenting by VLAN tag alone without policy — network separation without default-deny enforcement between zones is decoration, not microsegmentation.
Common trap: granting service accounts standing privilege 'because CI/CD needs it' — pipelines need scoped, short-lived credentials per job, not eternal Domain Admin.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Zero Trust Architecture — Core concepts
concepts: Zero trust removes implicit trust from the network: no user, device, or workload is trusted based on location — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, per session.

NIST SP 800-207 frames this in tenets: all data sources are resources, all communication is secured regardless of location, access is granted per session by dynamic policy, and the enterprise continuously monitors asset integrity and posture.

The logical architecture has three parts: the policy engine (decides), the policy administrator (configures the decision into action), and the policy enforcement point (gates each resource) — identity and device signals feed the decision.
Microsegmentation contains lateral movement by enforcing least-privilege rules between workloads; software-defined perimeters hide resources entirely until access is brokered.
Zero trust is a program, not a product: any vendor selling 'zero trust in a box' is selling marketing. It is an ongoing architecture of identity, segmentation, and continuous verification.

example.code:
policy:
  resource: finance-app
  allow:
    - user.group: finance
      device.posture: compliant
      auth: phishing-resistant-mfa
  deny: default
example.walkthrough: A zero-trust policy states who (finance group), from what (compliant device), with how strong an authentication, may reach a resource — evaluated every session, default deny. Compare this to a firewall rule that only checks source IP: the policy engine sees identity and posture, not just packets.

pitfalls: Common trap: buying a 'zero trust' product and declaring victory — it is an architecture and operating model, not a SKU.
Common trap: equating VPN with zero trust — a VPN extends the trusted network; zero trust eliminates the concept.
Common trap: segmenting only north-south (perimeter) while leaving east-west flat — attackers live in east-west.
Common trap: authenticating once at login and never re-evaluating — sessions must reflect changing risk.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Zero Trust move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

lessons.title: Start Here: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: Three content types: lessons (concepts with worked examples), scenarios (timed decision drills — read the evidence before choosing), and labs (hands-on exercises with checks).
Work each domain as a triad: lessons first, then scenarios closed-book, then labs. The triad converts reading into doing.
Mock Assessment is your final exam — it draws from every domain at runtime. Attempt it only when every domain is green.
Note: this bootcamp contains two introductory domains ('zero-trust' and 'zerotrust') from its course history — both are valid; the new topical domains build on them.

example.code:
Worked example — a 60-minute study block
Setup: 25 min lessons → 20 min scenarios → 15 min lab.
Reasoning: Load the model, test recall under pressure, prove with work.
Takeaway: One triad pass per domain beats three passive re-reads.
example.walkthrough: Run one full triad on the NIST tenets domain today; log your three weakest topics.

pitfalls: Jumping to scenarios without lessons — the 'why' explanations assume lesson vocabulary.
Treating zero trust as a product: it is an architecture and a strategy, not a purchase.
Taking the mock first 'for a baseline' — it wastes your only dress rehearsal.
lessons.try_it: Pick a domain and complete its triad now.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: The Zero Trust Learning Loop
concepts: Learn in three layers: Layer 1 — the tenets and logical components (policy engine/administrator/enforcement point). Layer 2 — the mechanisms (identity, device posture, segmentation, encryption). Layer 3 — failure modes and migration realities.
For every lesson ask 'what breaks if this is missing?' Zero trust interviews are scenario-heavy: 'design access for contractors' or 'the VPN is gone, now what?'
Build a personal runbook: every lab's commands and every scenario's decision framework, written in your own words.
Revisit scenarios 48 hours after passing them. The tenets and the PE/PA/PEP component model are the classic fade-fast details.

example.code:
Worked example — the failure-mode habit
Setup: Lesson teaches microsegmentation.
Reasoning: Ask: 'What happens with flat network + strong identity? With segmentation + weak identity?'
Takeaway: Zero trust is layered — test each layer's absence to understand its value.
example.walkthrough: After each lesson, write three 'what breaks if...' questions and answer from memory.

pitfalls: Memorizing tenets without the component model — interviews ask how it WORKS, not just what it IS.
Studying mechanisms in isolation: real designs chain them (identity + device + segmentation).
Skipping migration planning: 'greenfield zero trust' is rare; brownfield migration is the job.
lessons.try_it: Start your runbook: one section per domain, decisions not just definitions.

lessons.title: What Interviews and Exams Actually Test
concepts: Interviewers test five things: the NIST tenets (can you name and apply them), identity-as-perimeter design, the VPN-to-ZTNA migration story, microsegmentation strategy, and continuous monitoring as the trust feedback loop.
Expect design scenarios: 'Our VPN is overloaded — propose the replacement.' Answers must show the component model (PE/PA/PEP), identity + device signals, and a migration path — not just 'buy ZTNA.'

Exam-style questions weight: the seven tenets, PE vs PA vs PEP roles, deployment models (device agent/gateway, enclave, resource portal), and trust-algorithm inputs (identity, device, behavior, resource sensitivity).
The differentiator: migration realism. 'We piloted on one app, measured, expanded' beats architectural poetry. The capstone gives you a real pilot story.

example.code:
Worked example — answering 'replace the VPN'
Setup: 500 remote users on an overloaded VPN.
Reasoning: Wrong: 'deploy ZTNA product X.' Right: inventory apps, identity foundation (SSO+MFA), pilot ZTNA on 2 apps, measure, expand; VPN retained only for the un-migratable remainder.
Takeaway: Migration thinking beats product naming.
example.walkthrough: Answer three scenarios aloud in 90 seconds each, whiteboard style.

pitfalls: Naming products instead of describing architecture — interviewers hire architects, not shoppers.
Forgetting the migration path: nobody rips out the VPN on day one.
No continuous-monitoring story: zero trust without feedback loops is just new walls.
lessons.try_it: Record yourself whiteboarding the PE/PA/PEP model from memory.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap: From Tenets to Pilot
concepts: Phase 1 — Foundations: nist-tenets, identity-perimeter, device-trust. Goal: explain the tenets, the component model, and identity/device-based access from memory.
Phase 2 — Enforcement: microsegmentation, ztna-architecture, data-protection. Goal: design network and data controls for a sample org.
Phase 3 — Operations: continuous-monitoring, zt-governance, migration-planning. Goal: plan a migration, define metrics, and govern the program.
Capstone: a zero trust PILOT for a real or realistic org — scoped, measured, documented. The pilot is your portfolio proof.
Pace: one phase per week, one triad per day.

example.code:
Worked example — phase gate
Setup: End of Phase 1.
Reasoning: Gate: whiteboard the 7 tenets + PE/PA/PEP, and design contractor access using identity+device signals.
Takeaway: Gates are provable skills.
example.walkthrough: Write your three phase-gate checklists now.

No capstone: 'I know zero trust' without a pilot design is unverifiable.
Ignoring governance: programs die without metrics and ownership.

lessons.title: Capstone Brief: Design a Zero Trust Pilot
concepts: Your capstone: a zero trust PILOT design for a realistic organization (use a fictional 300-person company or your lab): scope, architecture, migration waves, metrics, and governance — plus a working lab demo of the core mechanics.

Constraints that make it real: brownfield (existing VPN, AD, flat network), limited budget (phased, not big-bang), measurable outcomes (defined before starting), and an executive summary a CIO would read.

Deliverables: current-state assessment, target architecture (PE/PA/PEP mapped to real components), 3 migration waves, metrics dashboard design, risk register, and a lab demo (identity-aware access to one app).
Grading: would this survive 'how much does wave 1 cost?' and 'what do we do about the legacy app that cannot do SSO?'

example.code:
Worked example — the pilot narrative
Setup: 'Show me wave 1.'
Reasoning: Wave 1: SSO+MFA for all humans + ZTNA pilot on the CRM (50 users) + device compliance check. Success metric: VPN sessions for CRM drop 80%; helpdesk auth tickets tracked.
Takeaway: A pilot is a bounded experiment with a hypothesis and a measurement.
example.walkthrough: Write your capstone brief: org profile, scope, constraints, success metrics.

pitfalls: Designing for a greenfield that does not exist: brownfield constraints are the assignment.
No metrics: a pilot without measurements is a project, not an experiment.
Boiling the ocean: wave 1 must be shippable in a quarter.
lessons.try_it: Draft the one-page executive summary first — if it does not fit, the scope is wrong.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: Mapping PE/PA/PEP to Reality
concepts: The logical model: Policy Engine (trust decision), Policy Administrator (executes: configure PEPs), Policy Enforcement Point (the gate: gateway, agent, proxy). Map each to REAL components in your design.

Example mapping: PE = identity provider + device-compliance engine + risk engine evaluating signals; PA = the ZTNA controller / policy orchestrator; PEP = the access proxy/gateway or endpoint agent enforcing per-session decisions.
Data flows: subject → PEP → PA (with PE decision) → resource. Every flow authenticated, authorized per-session, encrypted. Draw it for your pilot app.
Trust algorithm inputs for YOUR org: identity strength, device posture, behavior baseline, resource sensitivity, threat intel. Define what each contributes and what overrides.

example.code:
Worked example — the contractor flow
Setup: Contractor needs the CRM.
Reasoning: PEP (access proxy) challenges → PA asks PE: identity (contractor, MFA'd?) + device (compliant? EDR healthy?) + resource (CRM = medium sensitivity) → allow with session recording, 4h limit.
Takeaway: Every access is a fresh decision on fresh signals.
example.walkthrough: Draw your PE/PA/PEP mapping with real product categories (not just vendor names).

pitfalls: PE/PA/PEP as buzzwords with no mapping: the model must touch real components.
One static decision at login: zero trust decides per-session, continuously.
Ignoring the legacy app: document its compensating controls explicitly.
lessons.try_it: Write the trust-algorithm input table for your pilot: signals, sources, weights.

lessons.title: Capstone Verification: Measuring the Pilot
concepts: Define success BEFORE wave 1: e.g., phishing-success rate on pilot users, mean time to provision/deprovision, VPN bandwidth reduction, unauthorized-access attempts blocked, audit finding closure.
Instrument: the metrics need data sources (IdP logs, ZTNA gateway logs, EDR, SIEM). A metric without a source is a wish.
Report like an executive: before/after, trend, and 'what we learned.' Pilots that cannot show results do not get wave 2 funding.
Capture failure too: what did not work, what was harder than expected, what you would change. Honest retrospectives are the most credible artifact.

example.code:
Worked example — the metrics table
Setup: Wave 1 pilot, 50 users.
Reasoning: Metric: CRM access via VPN (before: 50 users/day; after: 8) — source: VPN + ZTNA logs. Metric: auth-related tickets (before: 12/wk; after: 5) — source: helpdesk.
Takeaway: Two honest metrics beat ten vanity ones.
example.walkthrough: Define 5 pilot metrics with sources and targets now.

pitfalls: Vanity metrics: 'users migrated' without security-outcome measures.
No baseline: measure BEFORE wave 1 or 'improvement' is fiction.
Hiding the failures: the retrospective is where the learning (and credibility) lives.
lessons.try_it: Build the before/after dashboard mockup for your pilot.

lessons.title: Never Trust, Always Verify: The Core Tenet in Practice
concepts: 'Never trust, always verify' means: no access decision based on network location, ever. Every request — user, device, workload — is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, per session.
In practice: the VPN's 'inside = trusted' model is replaced by identity + device + context evaluated at a policy enforcement point, for each resource, each session.
Verify explicitly: use ALL available signals (identity strength, device health, location, behavior, resource sensitivity) — not just the password that got them in.
This tenet is the interview answer to 'what is zero trust in one sentence' — but you must be able to show what changes operationally: per-request auth, no implicit zones.

example.code:
Worked example — the VPN replacement
Setup: Remote user needs the ERP.
Reasoning: Old: VPN → trusted LAN → ERP. New: identity (MFA) + device (compliant) verified at the access proxy → per-session ERP access only.
Takeaway: The network location stopped being a credential.
example.walkthrough: Explain to a colleague what changes for THEM when the VPN goes away.

pitfalls: 'Zero trust = no VPN': it is no IMPLICIT trust; remote access still exists, rebuilt on identity.
Verifying once at login: 'always' means continuous, per-session re-evaluation.
Applying it to users but not workloads: service accounts need verification too.
lessons.try_it: Map one of your own daily accesses to the verify-explicitly model.

lessons.title: Assume Breach: Designing for the Inevitable
concepts: 'Assume breach' is an engineering assumption: design as if an attacker is already inside. It drives segmentation (limit lateral movement), least privilege (limit what stolen creds can do), and monitoring (detect fast).

Practical consequences: flat networks are unacceptable (blast radius = everything), standing admin rights are pre-authorized breach material (use just-in-time), and detection must be fast (dwell time is the metric).
It is not defeatism: assuming breach focuses investment where it matters — containment and detection — instead of on a perimeter that will be bypassed.
Test it: red-team exercises and breach simulations validate whether 'assume breach' is architecture or just a slide.

example.code:
Worked example — the phished credential
Setup: Attacker has a valid user password.
Reasoning: Without assume-breach: VPN + password = full LAN. With it: MFA blocks the login; even with session theft, microsegmentation contains movement and EDR flags the anomaly.
Takeaway: Each layer assumes the previous one failed.
example.walkthrough: Run a tabletop: 'attacker has a valid password' — what stops them in your design?

pitfalls: Assume breach without segmentation: the assumption with no engineering behind it.
Treating it as a mindset only: it must produce concrete controls.
Assuming breach of OTHERS but not your own admin paths: attackers love admin tools.
lessons.try_it: List three controls in your environment that exist BECAUSE of assume-breach.

lessons.title: Least Privilege: Temporal and Scoped
concepts: Least privilege has two axes: SCOPE (only the resources needed) and TIME (only for as long as needed). Standing 24/7 admin rights fail both.
Just-in-time access: elevate for the task, auto-expire after. The credential exists for hours, not years — stolen creds have a short half-life.
Just-enough access: the narrowest role that completes the task. Break-glass procedures cover the exceptional, not the routine.
Measure it: percentage of accounts with standing privilege, average elevation duration, unused entitlements. Least privilege is a metric, not a vibe.

example.code:
Worked example — the DBA's access
Setup: DBA needs prod DB access.
Reasoning: Old: standing sysadmin. New: JIT elevation for the change window (4h), scoped to the one database, MFA'd, session-recorded, auto-revoked.
Takeaway: The access exists exactly as long as the need.
example.walkthrough: Audit one privileged account: scope, duration, last used. Right-size it.

pitfalls: JIT without approval workflow: self-service elevation with no oversight is standing access with extra steps.
Scoping by role title: roles accrete; review entitlements against actual usage.
Exempting 'emergency' accounts permanently: break-glass must be monitored, not invisible.
lessons.try_it: Implement JIT for one admin workflow this month.

lessons.title: Policy Engine, Administrator, and Enforcement Point
